The mountains here are old and weathered, less volcanically active than Hi but no less formidable -- steep valleys, narrow passes, and ridgelines that catch storms rolling in from the southern sea.

The southern mountains are resource-rich -- mineral deposits, timber in the sheltered valleys, and stone quarried from exposed cliff faces. But the terrain resists large-scale settlement. Communities are small, isolated by geography, and accustomed to self-reliance.

The Tsuchikawa (Earth River) is the main artery -- wide, slow, navigable for cargo barge travel, and historically important as a trade route connecting the interior to the coast.

Tsuchimoto sits at the center of the provincial plains, connected by roads in every compass direction. It is not a dramatic city -- no spectacular geography, no great harbor. It is a city of markets, granaries, administrative buildings, and the quietly enormous power of whoever controls the food supply.

Points of Interest:

  • The Great Granaries of Tsuchimoto -- Immense storage structures capable of holding enough grain to feed Hokori's population through two years of failed harvests. One of the most strategically important sites in the archipelago.
  • The Buried Road -- An ancient paved road that farmers have plowed around for centuries. Predates the Emperor's Highway by thousands of years -- pre-imperial, possibly pre-human. Where it goes and why it exists is unknown.

Settlements

Settlement Type Notes
Tsuchimoto City Agricultural capital; granary city; market center; Genso-aligned
Tashiro Town River town; barge trade; grain export hub
Komugi Village "Wheat"; small farming commune; exemplary agricultural management
Inaka Village Meaning literally "countryside"; deliberately generic; culturally proud of it

Culture & Trade

Tsuchi's culture reflects its agricultural identity -- practical, organized, and deeply connected to the land and seasons. The province's grain production is a strategic asset that gives its governing authority disproportionate political leverage. River trade along the Tsuchikawa connects the interior to coastal markets.

History

Tsuchi has long been Hokori's breadbasket. Its strategic importance has made it a prize in every major conflict. The province's current Genso Alliance alignment gives the alliance control over a significant portion of Hokori's food supply -- a fact with profound implications for the current political crisis.

• The Buried Road leads somewhere significant -- it is far older than any known human construction in the region.
  • The Great Granaries' contents are being used as an economic weapon in the current conflict.

The Granaries as Political Weapon

The Genso Alliance-aligned governing clan has been quietly restricting grain sales to Arashi-aligned provinces while maintaining normal trade with neutral parties. This is a slow-moving economic siege strategy. It hasn't become visible yet. When it does, it will escalate the current conflict significantly.

The Buried Road

The ancient road leads eventually to a pre-imperial site associated with the Emerald Dragon Clan (Midoryu) -- a "green court" predating any recorded human settlement. Traceable sections exist at intervals. The site it leads to is in the Kusa province border region, beneath what is now part of the Whispering Flats. Midoryu is alive and maintains a particular connection to this buried court.

Plot Hooks

  • A farmer plowing a new field in eastern Tsuchi has found an intact structure beneath the buried road -- a sealed room -- and reported it to local authorities; those authorities are now not responding to outside inquiries
  • The granary administrator in Tsuchimoto is receiving death threats; she has information about grain supply restrictions that she wants to share with someone she trusts -- which is no one, currently

locations.name: The Zasu's Ritual Scrolls — Hebi no Hensen

text.content:
Type
location-item
Status
active

Found on or near the Nagaji Zasu's body after the encounter in the Inner Sanctum (Room 6). A bundle of documents carried by the creature — some rolled tightly inside a cracked leather scroll case lashed to the body with strips of torn silk, others loose and partially crushed beneath its coils.

Physical Description:

The scroll case is lacquered hardwood, once fine, now split along one seam and discoloured by sustained contact with scaled flesh. It is lashed to the Zasu's midsection with strips of silk torn from what was once a formal obi — deep indigo fabric with a barely visible mon: a crescent moon above still water.

Inside: seven documents in varying states of preservation. Not a single unified text — a collection, assembled from multiple sources over time. Some are written in the same hand. Others are not.

The Bundle:

  1. Three intact sheets — Heavy mulberry paper, brushwork in formal seimaster notation. Dense. Technical. Written in a dialect of Classical Kagekunian that predates the current era by centuries. Not a language any living scholar would read fluently, but structural elements are recognizable to anyone trained in arcane or historical study.

  2. One large diagram — Folded repeatedly and worn soft at the creases. Ink faded at the edges but the central image is clear: a human figure enclosed in concentric rings of notation, with lines radiating outward to seven points. The figure's outline blurs at the extremities — the arms taper, the legs merge, the head elongates. Whether this depicts a process or a result is not immediately clear.

  3. Two damaged pages — Charred along one edge, as though pulled from a fire before the damage was complete. The surviving text is fragmentary. Diagrams of something anatomical — bones? Muscles? The proportions are wrong for a human body. Marginal annotations in a second, more hurried hand.

  4. One loose leaf — Thinner paper, different ink, different hand entirely. A list or index of some kind — short entries, each followed by a location reference and a symbol. Several entries have been circled. One has been crossed out with a single deliberate stroke.

Investigation & Identification

  • Identify the scroll case's origin (DC 12 Investigation)
  • Identify the obi fabric and mon (DC 13 Investigation or DC 11 History with Gekkō knowledge)
  • Read the intact sheets — surface meaning (DC 14 Arcana)
  • Read the intact sheets — deeper understanding (DC 17 Arcana)
  • Interpret the large diagram (DC 13 Arcana or DC 14 Medicine)
  • Read the damaged pages (DC 15 Arcana; DC 13 if diagram already interpreted)
  • Interpret the loose leaf index (DC 14 Investigation)
  • Identify the crossed-out entry (DC 16 History or DC 14 with Ko'jiri's Golden Dragon advantage)
  • Recognize the reversal reference (DC 18 Arcana; DC 15 if intact sheets already read at deeper understanding)

Check Results

The Scroll Case — DC 12 Investigation: The case itself is seimaster's equipment — purpose-built for transporting documents that carry active sei residue. The interior is lined with a thin copper-leaf layer designed to insulate the contents from ambient magical interference. This is not a general-purpose scroll case. It was made for carrying something dangerous, or at least something that interacted with sei in ways that required containment.

The Obi and Mon — DC 13 Investigation (or DC 11 History with prior Gekkō knowledge): The silk is from a formal obi — the width, weave, and indigo dye are consistent with dress worn by clan leadership or senior retainers during official functions. The mon embroidered into the fabric is a crescent moon reflected in still water. Any character who has encountered Clan Gekkō's heraldry — or studied the independent clans — recognizes this as the Gekkō clan crest. The Zasu was carrying documents bound to its body with a strip of its own formal clothing.

The Intact Sheets — DC 14 Arcana (Surface Reading): The notation system is recognizable as seimaster technical writing — the equivalent of a magical research language. The three sheets describe a process. Something is being channelled through a living subject. The terminology is archaic but the structural grammar matches transformation magic — not illusion, not transmutation in the temporary sense, but permanent alteration of a living form. References to "the vessel" and "the shape beyond" appear repeatedly. The tone is clinical. There is no ethical framing anywhere in the text — no discussion of consent, consequence, or reversal. It reads like instructions, not philosophy.

The Intact Sheets — DC 17 Arcana (Deeper Understanding): At this level of comprehension, specific details emerge. The transformation described is not a single event but a cascading process — once initiated in one subject, it propagates through sei-bonded individuals in proximity. The ritual was designed for a group, not an individual. The source tradition is not Golden Dragon — the foundational theory, the sei-alignment patterns, the structural logic all point to Kokuryu. Onyx Dragon magical tradition. A character who knows anything about the dragon clans understands immediately: this was never Kinryū's work. Someone found Kokuryu research and tried to use it.

The text also references a prerequisite — a "site of origin" where the sei conditions are correct for the initial casting. The site is not named. But the geographic and environmental markers described (acoustic distortion, thermal anomalies, hollow stone formations) do not match any location the party has visited. They match somewhere else. Somewhere in Kaze Province.

The Large Diagram — DC 13 Arcana or DC 14 Medicine: The figure at the center is human. The process depicted moves outward through the concentric rings — each ring representing a stage. The outermost ring shows a form that is no longer human. Limbs have fused. The spine has elongated. The skull has narrowed and stretched. A medical eye (DC 14 Medicine) recognizes that this is not artistic abstraction — the anatomical transitions are rendered with the precision of someone who understood exactly how a human body would need to change to arrive at the depicted result. The seven radiating points correspond to sei meridian nodes in the body — the same points targeted in advanced healing magic, but inverted. Whatever this process does, it rewrites the subject at the level of their sei architecture. There is no "off" described anywhere on the diagram.

The Damaged Pages — DC 15 Arcana (DC 13 if diagram already interpreted): Fragmentary, but enough survives to understand: these pages describe what happens after the transformation. Behavioral changes. Cognitive deterioration over time — described not as a flaw but as a known parameter. The phrase that survives most completely translates roughly as: "the mind narrows to the form." A character who has already interpreted the diagram understands: the transformation was known to degrade rational thought. Whoever designed this ritual documented the cognitive cost and included it anyway. The annotations in the second hand — more hurried, less formal — appear to be someone's attempt to calculate timelines. How long before the subject loses coherent speech. How long before decision-making capacity degrades below functional thresholds. The numbers are partially burned away, but the progression described is measured in months, not years.

The Loose Leaf Index — DC 14 Investigation: A reference list. Each entry consists of a short descriptor (a place or a thing, not a person), a location reference using a coordinate system the party does not recognize, and a symbol from a set of about a dozen recurring glyphs. The format is consistent with a research index — a scholar's shorthand for tracking source materials across multiple sites. Several entries have been circled in the same ink as the intact sheets. One entry — near the bottom of the list — has been crossed out with a single, deliberate horizontal stroke. The ink used for the strike-through is different from everything else on the page. Newer.

The Crossed-Out Entry — DC 16 History (DC 14 with Ko'jiri's Golden Dragon Clan advantage): The struck entry's descriptor translates loosely as "the golden restoration" or "the golden counter-work." Its location reference, while in the same unrecognized coordinate system as the rest, includes a secondary notation that uses directional language consistent with mountain-interior positioning. A character with knowledge of the Golden Dragon Clan's history (Ko'jiri) recognizes the phrasing: "counter-work" is a term used in Golden Dragon magical tradition for a specifically developed countermeasure to another clan's magic. The crossed-out entry refers to a Golden Dragon response to whatever this ritual represents. It exists — or existed — somewhere. And whoever crossed it out knew it was there and chose to mark it as eliminated, completed, or irrelevant.

The Reversal Reference — DC 18 Arcana (DC 15 if intact sheets already read at deeper understanding): Buried in the technical language of the intact sheets, between two passages describing sei-channel alignment during the transformation's second phase, is a parenthetical notation — almost an aside. It translates approximately as: "Restoration of original form requires inversion at the site of origin, using the counter-work of the golden tradition, during a convergence of the three lights." Three components. A location (site of origin — wherever the ritual was first performed). A method (the Golden Dragon countermeasure — the crossed-out entry on the index). A timing condition (convergence of the three lights — a celestial alignment involving Kagekuni's three stars). The notation is not a guide. It is a footnote — an acknowledgement that reversal is theoretically possible, recorded with the clinical detachment of someone cataloguing edge cases, not someone who expected it to matter.

DM Notes

Why the Zasu carries these: The chief seimaster gathered these documents before performing the ritual on himself — the last to undergo it, trying to maintain enough awareness to lead his transformed people. He kept them because some fragment of the scholar he was still compels him to. The scrolls are lashed to his body the way a drowning person holds a rope. He cannot read them anymore. He cannot remember why they matter. But he will not let them go.

The obi: The strip of formal clothing binding the case to the Zasu's body is a detail that should land quietly. This creature dressed itself. Or — more precisely — something that was becoming this creature took the time to secure these documents to its body using a piece of its own ceremonial clothing before the transformation completed. The crescent moon mon is facing outward. Whether that was intentional is unknowable.

Narrative function: These scrolls serve three purposes simultaneously:

  1. Dot-connection for the Gekkō investigation. The Gekkō mon on the obi, the transformation ritual in the sheets, and the Nagaji the party has been fighting begin to form a single picture. The party doesn't need to reach the full conclusion here — but they should leave this encounter with a growing unease that the Nagaji are not what they assumed.

  2. Breadcrumb toward the Order of the Black Lily. The "site of origin" referenced in the reversal notation — with its acoustic distortion, thermal anomalies, and hollow stone — describes a location in Kaze Province. The party doesn't know that yet. When they reach Kaze and encounter those geographic features, the scrolls become a key that unlocks a door they didn't know they were carrying.

  3. Breadcrumb toward the Golden Dragon countermeasure. The crossed-out entry on the index tells the party two things: a reversal exists (or existed), and someone — the Zasu, before the transformation — knew about it and struck it from the list. Whether he crossed it out because he believed it was destroyed, because he had already looked for it and failed, or because he wanted to ensure no one pursued it, is deliberately ambiguous. The party may interpret this differently depending on their read of the Zasu — as a warning, a surrender, or a sabotage.

What the scrolls do NOT reveal:

  • They do not name Clan Gekkō, Masota Gekkō, or any individual
  • They do not explain why the ritual was performed
  • They do not describe where the "site of origin" is (geographic markers only — no place names)
  • They do not confirm that the Nagaji the party has fought are transformed people (the connection is inferential, not explicit)
  • They do not provide enough information to perform the reversal — only to know that one theoretically exists and requires three components the party does not yet have

Ko'jiri's unique position: Ko'jiri's advantage on Golden Dragon History checks makes him the most likely party member to identify the crossed-out entry's significance. This is by design — the con artist who faked Golden Dragon expertise is now the person whose genuine research matters most. If Ko'jiri is the one who identifies the "golden counter-work" reference, the narrative irony completes: the knowledge he built to deceive is the knowledge that may save an entire clan.

Timing and pacing: The scrolls are meant to be studied, not instantly decoded. Encourage the party to examine them over a short rest or between encounters. The check DCs are set so that a single character is unlikely to extract everything in one pass — this is a puzzle that rewards collaboration. The fighter won't read the Arcana. The sorcerer won't catch the History. The druid might notice the Medicine angle on the diagram. Everyone has something to contribute, and the full picture only emerges when they share what they've found.

frontmatter.name: The Zasu's Ritual Scrolls — Hebi no Hensen

text.content:
Type
core

The people of Kagekuni use "bakemono" as a broad term for anything that is neither person nor beast in any familiar sense — the changed things, the hungry things, the things that should not be where they are. Scholars at the Seishin Enclave insist on finer taxonomy. Peasants in the valleys know the taxonomy doesn't matter when you hear breathing outside the shōji and there's nothing there.

What follows is organized by the categories most commonly used by seimasters and monster-hunters, though the boundaries between them blur more often than academics care to admit.

I. Yokai — The Changed Ones

Yokai are creatures of inherent supernatural nature — not spirits of the dead, not divine, not ordinary beasts gone wrong. They exist because the world has room for them, because sei flows through living things and some living things are stranger than others. Most yokai are intelligent. Many are ancient. A few are friendly, though "friendly" is a relative term when the creature in question can swallow a horse.

Oni

The great horned demons of Kagekuni are as much a part of the mountains as the stone itself. They come in colors — red, blue, black, green — and each color carries different associations in local folklore, though the oni themselves don't seem to care what stories are told about them.

Oni are territorial, physical, and direct. They favor high places: mountain passes, cliff faces, abandoned fortifications. A lone oni will claim a stretch of road and exact tribute from travelers — food, sake, occasionally a fight for the sport of it. An oni band, which is rarer and more dangerous, will fortify a position and hold it against anything short of an army.

They are not stupid. An oni negotiating toll fees will remember a slight for decades. An oni given genuine respect — not fear, respect — may become a surprisingly reliable neighbor. Villages near known oni territory sometimes maintain formal arrangements: offerings left at specific stones on specific days, and in return the oni discourages bandits and worse things from using the same road.

During the sei drought, oni populations declined sharply. Many retreated underground or fell into torpor. Since the Great Awakening, sightings have risen steadily, and some oni have emerged disoriented and aggressive after millennia of sleep — a problem for the settlements that grew up in their territory while they slumbered.

Tengu

Tengu inhabit the deep mountain forests and high ridgelines where the canopy thins and the wind carries the smell of pine resin and distant snow. They appear as tall, thin humanoids with corvid features — black-feathered wings, sharp dark eyes, beaked faces that manage to convey expressions no beak should be capable of.

They are warriors without peer. The legendary swordsmanship schools of Kagekuni trace their lineage to tengu instructors, and the debt is not metaphorical — tengu did teach human swordsmen, centuries ago, and some still do. A tengu who deems a mortal worthy of instruction will appear uninvited, train the student to the point of exhaustion and beyond, then vanish without explanation. The student is expected to understand the lesson eventually. Tengu do not explain themselves.

Tengu society is hierarchical and secretive. The greater tengu — the Daitengu — are beings of considerable power, rumored to command weather and move through sei as birds move through air. The lesser tengu, the Kotengu, are more numerous and more volatile: tricksters, thieves, and occasional allies who delight in humbling the proud and rewarding the humble. They are particularly fond of embarrassing monks whose piety exceeds their actual virtue.

Kitsune

Fox spirits. The most well-known and most misunderstood of the yokai.

A kitsune appears, in its natural form, as a fox of unusual size and intelligence with fur that may be red, white, silver, or — in the oldest and most powerful — gold. They are shapeshifters who can assume human form with enough skill to pass undetected for years or even decades. The number of tails a kitsune possesses reflects its age and power: a young kitsune has one; the legendary nine-tailed elders are beings of near-divine potency.

Kitsune are drawn to interesting people and interesting situations, which makes them unpredictable. Some serve as guardians of specific places — shrines, crossroads, ancient groves. Others attach themselves to mortals out of curiosity, affection, or an amusement that can look identical to malice from the outside. A kitsune's gifts always come with complications. A kitsune's tricks always contain a lesson, though the lesson may not become clear for years.

They are deeply tied to the spirit world and to sei. Kitsune illusions are not mere glamour — they reshape perception at a fundamental level, and a sufficiently powerful kitsune can make the illusory real, if only temporarily. Fire is their traditional element: foxfire, the cold blue flame that marks kitsune territory, burns without heat but illuminates things that ordinary light cannot reveal.

The foothills of the Tenchūsan Ren are known to harbor at least one kitsune of considerable age who has occupied the same burrow system for approximately two centuries. She is aware of the landmarks referenced in certain old documents and finds this mildly amusing.

Tanuki

The raccoon-dogs of Kagekuni are shapeshifters like kitsune, but where kitsune are elegant and calculating, tanuki are exuberant, gluttonous, and absolutely shameless. A tanuki disguised as a merchant will sell you leaves that look like gold coins — and the deception will hold just long enough for the tanuki to spend the real coins you gave as change on sake and tempura.

Tanuki are social creatures who gather in loose communities near human settlements, drawn by the availability of food, drink, and entertainment. They are excellent mimics, passable musicians, and terrible liars who succeed anyway through sheer confidence and the fact that people don't expect a pot-bellied creature with a leaf on its head to be running an elaborate confidence scheme.

Despite their reputation as comic figures, tanuki are not harmless. An angry tanuki can reshape its body into something much larger and much less amusing. A tanuki protecting its young will fight with a ferocity that surprises creatures who only know the jolly sake-drinking version. And old tanuki — the ones who have lived long enough to stop caring whether anyone finds them funny — are shapeshifters of alarming skill who can maintain disguises indefinitely and have been known to replace village headmen for months without detection.

Jorogumo

The spider-women of the deep forests and abandoned estates. A jorogumo appears as a beautiful woman — or as an enormous spider the size of a small horse — and the transition between the two forms is disturbingly fluid. They spin webs of silk so fine it catches light like water, and their lairs are decorated with an aesthetic sensibility that would be admirable if the decorations didn't include the drained husks of previous visitors.

Jorogumo are patient, intelligent, and profoundly solitary. They claim territories — a ruined villa, a cave behind a waterfall, a particular stretch of forest path — and weave elaborate traps for anything that wanders in. Their webs conduct sei, and a jorogumo sitting at the center of her web can feel vibrations from hundreds of feet away, reading the approach of prey through tremors in the silk.

They are not mindless predators. A jorogumo who has recently fed may invite a traveler to tea, make polite conversation, and allow them to leave unharmed — though she will remember their face and their scent, and if they return she will expect them to bring a gift. Jorogumo appreciate poetry, fine fabric, and musical skill. They despise dishonesty, which is ironic given that their primary hunting strategy is deception.

Nure-Onna

The wet women of rivers and coastal marshes. They appear as women from the waist up, with the body of an enormous serpent below — though they can compress their lower form enough to wade through shallows and appear merely waist-deep in water. Their hair is perpetually wet and black as lacquer, and their faces are beautiful in the specific way that a riptide is beautiful: compelling and absolutely lethal.

Nure-onna haunt river crossings, bridges, and tidal flats. Their preferred method is to appear holding a bundle wrapped in cloth and crying for help — a lost child, a drowning infant. When a compassionate traveler approaches and takes the bundle, it becomes impossibly heavy, pinning them in place while the nure-onna strikes. The bundle contains nothing but river stones and malice.

They are territorial and aggressive, and unlike many yokai, they show little interest in conversation or negotiation. A river known to harbor a nure-onna will be marked with warning shimenawa by local villagers, and fords will be relocated upstream at considerable expense rather than risk the crossing.

Tsukumogami

Objects that have existed for one hundred years and, through long use and the slow accumulation of sei, have awakened into something like consciousness. A tea kettle that hops off its hook at midnight. An umbrella that opens itself in sunshine and closes in rain, spitefully. A writing brush that produces calligraphy of startling beauty when no one is holding it.

Tsukumogami are the most common yokai in Kagekuni, though most go unrecognized. They are minor spirits — rarely dangerous, frequently annoying, occasionally helpful. A household that treats its tools and implements with respect will find them lasting longer and working better; a household that is careless with its possessions may wake one morning to find every pot in the kitchen rearranged and the broom hiding behind the woodpile.

Since the Great Awakening, the rate of tsukumogami manifestation has increased noticeably. Seimasters debate whether this reflects higher ambient sei, accumulated potential finally expressing after the drought, or simply that people are paying closer attention. Whatever the cause, households across Kagekuni are discovering that their grandmother's mirror has opinions about its placement.

II. Yurei & the Restless Dead

Death in Kagekuni is not always permanent, and it is rarely clean. The dead who linger do so because something binds them — an oath unfulfilled, a wrong unavenged, a love that outlasted the body. They are called yurei, and they are treated with a mixture of pity, fear, and practical concern.

Yurei

The classic restless dead. They appear in white burial kimono, hair unbound, feet that do not quite touch the ground. Their forms are translucent but visible, and the temperature drops in their presence — a cold that settles into the bones and does not leave quickly.

Yurei are bound to specific places, people, or purposes. A yurei haunting the place of their death may replay their final moments endlessly, unaware of the living. A yurei seeking vengeance will pursue their target with patient, relentless focus, appearing at the edges of rooms and in reflections until the moment they strike. A yurei bound by love will simply... wait, in the place where they were happiest, for a reunion that may never come.

The most dangerous yurei are those who have forgotten why they linger. Their original purpose has been satisfied or has become meaningless, but the binding holds. These confused dead become increasingly hostile over time, lashing out at the living not from malice but from a formless anguish they can no longer articulate.

Proper funeral rites prevent most hauntings. Shrines dedicated to ancestor veneration help maintain the boundary. When a yurei does manifest, the most reliable resolution is to identify and address the binding cause — which may require investigation, negotiation, or acts of restitution that the living find inconvenient.

Bōrei

A bōrei is a yurei of unusual potency — a spirit whose binding is so strong, whose will was so defined in life, that they persist with something approaching full consciousness. They can speak, reason, and in some cases interact physically with the world around them. They do not decay in the way lesser yurei do; a bōrei may haunt a place for centuries without losing coherence.

Bōrei are rare and significant. A bōrei in a temple was almost certainly someone of great devotion or authority. A bōrei in a castle was likely a lord or general whose duty extended past death. They can be communicated with — carefully — and may possess knowledge that no living person retains.

The inner sanctum of Ōryūzan Tenkū-ji is known to house such a spirit: the translucent figure of a priest still seated at his writing desk, still keeping records in a chamber where the torchlight dims but does not extinguish.

Gashadokuro

The great skeletons. When a mass death occurs — a battle, a famine, a plague — and the dead are not properly honored, the accumulated resentment of the forgotten coalesces into a single enormous skeletal figure, fifteen to twenty feet tall, assembled from the bones of the unburied. A gashadokuro makes no sound except the faint rattle of its joints and the grinding of its teeth. It hunts at night, drawn to the living by the warmth of their blood, and it bites the heads off its victims with a casualness that borders on contempt.

They are extraordinarily difficult to destroy. Scattering the bones only delays the reassembly. The only permanent solution is to identify the mass death that created it and perform proper funerary rites for every victim — a task that may require historical research, excavation, and the cooperation of priests who would rather not dig up battlefields.

The civil war has generated conditions ripe for gashadokuro formation. Border skirmishes with unmarked graves, villages burned without survivors to perform the rites, soldiers lost in mountain passes where the bodies are never recovered — each is a potential origin point. The fact that no gashadokuro have been reported yet may mean the accumulation hasn't reached critical mass, or it may mean the sightings haven't been believed.

Gaki

Hungry ghosts. The dead who were consumed by greed, gluttony, or obsession in life return as gaki — emaciated, translucent figures with distended bellies and mouths too small to eat. They cluster around sources of what they craved: food markets, treasure houses, sake breweries. They cannot consume what they desire; the attempt to do so causes them visible agony, which they repeat compulsively.

Gaki are pathetic more than dangerous, but in large numbers they create an aura of gnawing hunger that affects the living — food spoils faster, drink tastes of ash, and the feeling of being perpetually unsatisfied settles over anyone who lingers too long. Gaki clusters near famine sites or abandoned marketplaces are a recognized hazard, and traveling monks sometimes perform the rites of feeding — offering symbolic sustenance that, while it doesn't satisfy the gaki, briefly eases their suffering enough to thin the cluster.

III. Sei-Touched — The Changed and the Changing

Sei does not merely fuel magic. It saturates the world, and where it pools or flows in concentrated currents, the things that live in those currents change. The sei drought suppressed this process for three millennia. Since the Great Awakening, it has resumed — and the world is still adjusting.

Sei Beasts

Ordinary animals exposed to elevated sei concentrations over time. The changes are cumulative and unpredictable: a deer in the Yōsei Mori might grow a third eye that perceives sei flows, or develop antlers of crystallized amber that resonate in the presence of magic. A hawk nesting near a sei wellspring might produce offspring with feathers of metallic bronze that cut like razors.

Sei beasts are not inherently aggressive, but they are often territorial in ways their mundane counterparts are not, and their altered physiology can make them dangerous even without hostile intent. A sei-touched boar that generates localized tremors when it charges is not trying to hurt anyone — it's just running. The tremors are incidental. The fact that they can collapse a hillside is a separate problem.

The Yōsei Mori in Kusa province has the highest concentration of sei beasts in Hokori. Deeper reaches of the forest harbor creatures of significantly elevated intelligence — animals that plan, coordinate, and in some cases appear to communicate in ways that defy natural explanation. The Forest of Spirits faction maintains sanctuaries within the forest, and their relationship with these creatures is a subject of considerable speculation.

Sei Aberrations

When sei concentrations spike beyond what the local environment can integrate, the result is not gradual change but sudden, violent transformation. Sei aberrations are creatures — or were creatures — that have been overwhelmed by magical energy. Their bodies twist, merge with their surroundings, or develop properties that contradict their original nature: a fish that burns, a bird made of liquid stone, a tree that bleeds and screams when cut.

Sei aberrations are unpredictable and almost always hostile, not because they choose to be but because the transformation is agonizing and they lash out at anything nearby. They are most common near sei wellsprings, ley line intersections, and sites where magical catastrophes have occurred. The ruins of pre-Aphelion institutions — temples, laboratories, libraries — are particularly prone to aberration formation, as residual enchantments interact with returning sei in ways their builders never anticipated.

The Whispering Flats of Kusa province produce sounds that carry the qualities of speech — rhythmic, tonal, responsive to ambient conditions. Seimasters have debated for decades whether this constitutes a sei aberration, a natural phenomenon, or something else entirely. The sounds originate from a buried structure beneath the flats that has not been rediscovered.

Nagaji

Not a natural species. Nagaji are the result of a transformation ritual — specifically, a fragmentary rite tied to the Onyx Dragon Clan that was never meant to be performed with incomplete instructions. Those who undergo the ritual become serpentine humanoids: scaled, cold-blooded, driven by instincts they cannot fully suppress.

The transformation is progressive. In early stages, the subject retains most of their cognition but experiences intrusive impulses — a compulsion to seek warmth, to coil in enclosed spaces, to respond to threat with a stillness that precedes explosive violence. Over time, coherence degrades. The fully transformed communicate through a serpentine language to coordinate with each other, but whether they retain any memory of what they were is unclear.

Nagaji organize into squad structures — bushi, hohei, ashigaru, kannushi — that mirror military formations, suggesting either retained institutional memory or an instinctive social organization that converges on familiar patterns. The kannushi variants are drawn to sei-charged spaces and use meditation areas instinctively, hinting at a connection to whatever spiritual awareness the original ritual was meant to bestow.

The transformation is theoretically reversible. The requirements are extreme: the original ritual documentation, a specific sei configuration achievable only during a particular celestial alignment, and a practitioner capable of sei-based restoration at enormous scale. Whether any of these conditions can be met is an open question.

IV. Kami & Nature Spirits

Kami

Kami are minor spiritual beings that inhabit natural features — a particular waterfall, an ancient tree, a stone at a crossroads worn smooth by centuries of travelers' hands. They are not ghosts. They are not yokai. They are the spiritual expression of a place or thing that has accumulated enough presence, enough meaning, to develop something like awareness.

Most kami are subtle. A shrine maiden sweeping the steps of a waterfall shrine may feel the kami's approval as a faint warmth in the spray. A woodcutter who asks permission before felling a tree in a kami-touched grove may find his axe biting cleaner and his back aching less. A traveler who leaves an offering at a roadside stone may discover the weather holding fair for exactly as long as they need it to.

Kami do not speak, as a rule. They communicate through environmental response — a shift in wind, a change in light, the behavior of local animals. Interpreting these responses is an art form, and the shrine priests and miko who maintain kami relationships undergo years of training to read the signs correctly.

When angered — through desecration, neglect, or the destruction of their physical anchor — kami can become tatari-gami, spirits of curse and misfortune. A tatari-gami doesn't attack directly; it curdles luck. Crops fail. Children sicken. Tools break at the worst possible moment. The affliction continues until the offense is addressed, and addressing it requires first identifying which kami was offended and how — a process that can take months and may require specialist intervention.

Kodama

Tree spirits. Specifically, the spirits of trees old enough and significant enough to have developed individual awareness — a process that takes centuries in ordinary forests but may happen faster in sei-rich environments like the Yōsei Mori.

Kodama manifest as faint lights among the branches, as echoes that don't quite match the original sound, or — very rarely — as small humanoid figures of bark and leaf that watch from the canopy with expressions of ancient patience. A forest rich in kodama has a particular quality: sound carries differently, paths seem to shift between visits, and the feeling of being observed is constant and not entirely uncomfortable.

They are guardians of their groves. Kodama do not prevent logging — they are patient enough to understand that trees grow back — but they respond to wanton destruction with a hostility that manifests as navigational confusion, persistent bad weather over the affected area, and a gradual encroachment of roots and undergrowth that can reclaim cleared land within a single season.

V. Dragons & Dragon-kin

Dragons

The seven Progenitor Dragons founded the civilization of Kagekuni in the deep past. Their dragon clans — Crimson, Azure, Emerald, Onyx, Golden, Silver, and Amethyst — established the framework of society, religion, and magical practice that persists to this day, though the dragons themselves are remembered as historical and mythological figures rather than living beings.

Non-Progenitor dragons exist but are extraordinarily rare in the current era. Sightings occur perhaps once in a generation, usually in remote locations — the volcanic peaks of Fushichō, the deep waters around Kawa, the highest ridges of the Tenchūsan Ren. These encounters are poorly documented because the witnesses tend to be isolated travelers whose accounts are received with skepticism.

Dragon eggs are believed to be fossils — beautiful, collectible, and inert. They surface occasionally in excavations, in the hoards of other creatures, or in the treasure vaults of noble houses where they are displayed as relics of the founding era.

Ryūjin

Dragon-blooded beings. Not dragonborn — who are a distinct race claiming descent from the Progenitors — but creatures in which draconic blood manifests as something between beast and legend. A ryūjin might appear as an enormous serpent with vestigial wings, or a lizard the size of a war-horse with scales that refract light into colors that don't exist in the normal spectrum.

Ryūjin are tied to specific environments and elements. A river ryūjin commands the currents and can call floods or droughts. A mountain ryūjin causes tremors and rockslides, sometimes deliberately and sometimes as a byproduct of rolling over in its sleep. They are venerated in local tradition and placated with offerings, and the distinction between a ryūjin and a kami is a subject of ongoing theological debate.

VI. Mundane Wildlife

Kagekuni's natural fauna reflects the archipelago's varied geography — mountainous interiors, dense forests, river valleys, and extensive coastlines — filtered through the fundamental strangeness of Seizan.

Terrestrial

The forests of Hokori support populations of deer, boar, bear, fox, and wolf, along with smaller mammals that fill the expected ecological niches. What makes them Kagekuni's own is the cosmetic: deer with pelts that shift from copper to slate between seasons. Boar with bristles that carry a faint metallic sheen in certain light. Bears whose fur, when the animal is old enough, develops patches of deep indigo that no dye can replicate.

Mountain regions harbor snow monkeys in the heights, along with goats and ibex adapted to the thin air and crystalline terrain of the upper peaks. The Tenchūsan Ren is known for a large species of mountain cat — solitary, grey-furred, rarely seen — that local villages regard with superstitious respect and a practical desire to keep their livestock behind strong fences.

Avian

Cranes, herons, and egrets are common along waterways and are culturally significant — crane imagery appears in clan heraldry, religious iconography, and wedding ceremonies. Birds of prey include hawks, eagles, and a species of mountain falcon prized by the nobility for hunting. Corvids — crows, ravens, and jays — are ubiquitous and regarded with a wariness that reflects their association with tengu.

The forests support a variety of songbirds whose calls are distinct enough that experienced travelers use them for navigation and weather prediction. The nightjars of the Yōsei Mori produce a call that resonates with sei, creating a harmonic that skilled listeners can use to detect magical activity in the area — though whether the birds do this deliberately or incidentally is unknown.

Aquatic

The rivers and inland seas of Hokori support extensive freshwater fisheries. The goldtail fish — named for the iridescent gold flash of its tail fin — is commercially and culturally important, with seasonal runs during Aki that define the economic calendar of riverside settlements. Serenia-kai, the great inland sea, supports its own ecosystem of fish, crustaceans, and the occasional large predator whose exact nature is a matter of fishermen's debate.

Coastal waters harbor species familiar to any maritime culture — tuna, mackerel, octopus, various shellfish — alongside less explicable things. Deep-water fishermen report sightings of bioluminescent creatures at depth that do not correspond to any catalogued species, and the tidal caves of Umigakure are rumored to connect to a deeper cavity where something large enough to generate its own current has been detected by the disturbance patterns on the surface.

Insects & Minor Creatures

Fireflies in Kagekuni produce light in colors that shift with the season and, in sei-rich areas, with the phase of the nearest moon. Silk moths are commercially essential — the silk trade is a backbone of several provincial economies — and the moths themselves have been selectively bred for millennia, producing varieties that generate silk of unusual properties: threads that hold dye with preternatural permanence, fibers that resist rot, and in rare cases, silk that conducts sei in ways that interest the Seishin Enclave greatly.

Rats are opportunistic inhabitants of every ruin, cave, and settlement in the archipelago. They are unremarkable except in numbers, and the numbers can be considerable in abandoned structures where food stores have been left behind.

VII. Creatures of the Deep Past

Kagekuni is old. The Progenitor era stretches back over eight millennia, and the land was not empty before the dragons arrived. Occasionally, things surface — literally — that belong to epochs the historical record does not cover.

Pre-imperial ruins in remote locations sometimes contain guardian constructs that still function: stone figures that animate when specific thresholds are crossed, metal mechanisms that track intruders with eyeless heads, silk-wrapped bundles that unfold into something neither alive nor dead but very much still on duty. These constructs are powered by sei configurations that predate modern understanding, and the fact that they survived the three-thousand-year drought implies engineering of extraordinary sophistication or materials that store sei in ways current seimasters cannot replicate.

The buried structures beneath the Whispering Flats, the sealed foundations of the Stormwatch Cliffs, the deeper reaches of the Kagerō Gorge with its Onyx reliefs and disorienting sounds — all hint at a Kagekuni that existed before the clans, before the empire, before the current understanding of what sei is and what it can do. What lived in those places, and whether any of it still does, is not a question anyone has answered satisfactorily.

The temple complexes of the founding era — such as the ruins in the Tenchūsan Ren — were built with a sophistication of sei-integrated construction that current-era practitioners cannot replicate. The magic woven into their foundations is not battle magic or even enchantment in the conventional sense; it is foundational, structural, as though sei were used as a building material alongside stone and timber. What this implies about the creatures and entities that may have been bound into those structures as part of their construction is a question the party may want to consider before they go deeper.

frontmatter.name: Bakemono — Bestiary of Kagekuni
frontmatter.description: Creatures, yokai, spirits, sei-touched beasts, undead, and natural wildlife of the Shrouded Isles

text.content:
Type
core

Kagekuni's wilderness is rich with ingredients for those who know where to look. A competent traveler can supplement trail rations with foraged herbs, hunted game, and harvested fungi — and a skilled cook can transform these raw materials into meals that fortify the body and sharpen the mind.

the rarity terms to feel like grading vocabulary (how a cook or merchant would speak about ingredients

  • Common — 並 (Nami) — "regular, standard." This is the actual word used on Japanese restaurant menus for the base grade of nigiri, donburi, and unagi.
  • Uncommon — 上 (Jō) — "superior, upper." The next step up in the same grading system. Marks something better than ordinary but still attainable.
  • Rare — 特上 (Tokujō) — "special superior." A real grading term reserved for noticeably finer cuts and ingredients. Worth seeking out.
  • Very Rare — 極上 (Gokujō) — "supreme, finest." The top of the standard grading ladder. Anything above this leaves the language of grading entirely.
  • Legendary — 伝説 (Densetsu) — "legend." Steps out of the merchant's vocabulary and into the storyteller's. An ingredient that has stories attached to it.
  • Artifact — 神器 (Jingi) — "sacred vessel, divine treasure." This is the exact word used in Japanese mythology for the Imperial Regalia — the three sacred treasures of the Yamato dynasty. It carries the weight of Shinto cosmology and is the right register for something that sits between food and myth.

Gathering Rules

How Gathering Works

During travel or exploration, a character proficient in Survival may spend 1 hour foraging for ingredients. This can occur during a rest, while the party travels at a slow pace, or during dedicated downtime in a suitable environment.

The character makes a Wisdom (Survival) check. The DC depends on the terrain and the rarity of the ingredient sought.

Gathering DCs

DC Rarity Typical Yield
10 Common 1d4 portions of a common ingredient
13 Uncommon 1d3 portions of an uncommon ingredient
16 Rare 1d2 portions of a rare ingredient
20 Very Rare 1 portion of a very rare ingredient
— Legendary Cannot be foraged (see below)
— Artifact Cannot be foraged (see below)

A character who exceeds the DC by 5 or more finds an additional portion.

A character who fails by 5 or more in hazardous terrain triggers a complication — a poisonous lookalike gathered by mistake, an encounter with territorial wildlife, or a minor environmental hazard (slipping into a thermal vent, disturbing a spirit's resting place, etc.).

Legendary & Artifact Ingredients

Some ingredients exist beyond the reach of ordinary foraging. They cannot be found by scouring a hillside or stalking a forest, no matter how high the roll.

Legendary ingredients are one-of-a-kind harvests — cuts from a named creature slain once in the memory of a generation, a fruit that ripens on a single tree once per century, a reward bestowed by a figure who has the authority to bestow such things. They do not appear on gathering tables. They are obtained through story, not through the wilderness.

Legendary harvests from a named creature additionally require an exceptional skill check result to secure. When butchering or gathering from a source that could yield a Legendary ingredient, the cook must achieve a total of 40 or higher on the relevant check (Survival, Nature, or equivalent). Without the exceptional roll, the body yields only its rare and very rare cuts — the Legendary portion is either missed, spoiled in the harvest, or lost to the hand that did not know where to look.

This threshold is reachable only through the house rules already in play: a natural 20 on the d20 triggers a bonus d10 added to the roll, and session luck dice (1d4 generated each session) may be spent to push the total further. A proficient hunter with a strong Wisdom modifier, a natural 20, a high bonus die, and a luck expenditure can reach 40+ — but it will never be routine, and it will never be guaranteed. When it happens, it should feel earned.

Artifact ingredients sit at the border between food and myth. The flesh of a living Progenitor. The first rice of the first harvest. A vial of something drawn from a place that may not exist. Whether any such ingredient actually exists in the world is left to the DM, and whether the party ever encounters one is a campaign-defining decision. There are no mechanical rules for obtaining them — only the story that brought them into the cook's hands.

Gathering Modifiers

Condition Modifier
Character has herbalism kit +2 to foraging for herbs and fungi
Character has cook's utensils Advantage on identifying edible flora/fauna
Unfamiliar terrain (first time in province) -2
Guided by a local Advantage
Adverse weather (heavy rain, fog, snow) -2
Night foraging Disadvantage (unless darkvision)
Sei-active region (Yōsei Mori, near shrines) +2 to rare/very rare ingredients

Hunting Rules

Harvesting meat from wildlife uses the same hour-long activity but requires a Wisdom (Survival) check to track, followed by an appropriate combat or trap interaction to secure the kill. Butchering a carcass for usable meat requires 30 minutes and a DC 10 Survival or Nature check (failure wastes half the yield). Larger creatures yield more portions.

Creature Size Meat Yield
Small (rabbit, quail) 1–2 portions
Medium (deer, boar) 4–6 portions
Large (bear, elk) 8–12 portions

Bakemono and yokai are not safe to eat unless specifically noted. Sei-touched wildlife may produce unusual ingredients with additional properties — these are noted in the ingredient list below.

Fishing Rules

Fishing uses the same hour-long activity but requires a Wisdom (Survival) check with appropriate equipment (line, net, or improvised). Coastal and river fishing are distinct — a character familiar with one may be unfamiliar with the other. Tidal windows, seasonal runs, and water conditions affect availability.

Method Modifier Notes
Line and hook +0 Standard; requires bait or lure
Net (cast or drag) +2 Requires net; better for small fish and crabs
Spearfishing -2 No equipment needed beyond a sharp stick; favors clear water
Traps (overnight) +4 Must be set the previous day; risk of theft or animal interference

Ingredient Categories

I. Game & Fish — Niku (肉)

Common

Yama-usagi (Mountain Hare) Lean, dark meat found throughout Hokori's foothills and mountain passes. Plentiful along the Tenchūsan Ren and Sora's highland plateaus. Mild flavor, takes seasoning well. Terrain: Mountains, foothills, highland grassland Yield: 1–2 portions per hare Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Kawa-gani (River Crab) Small freshwater crabs found in streams and rivers across Hana, Mizu, and Kusa. Sweet, delicate meat extracted from the claws. Children in farming villages catch them as a common snack. Terrain: Rivers, streams, rice paddies Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of gathering Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Uzura (Quail) Ground-nesting birds common in the grasslands of Kusa and the lowland fields of Tsuchi. Easy to trap, quick to prepare. A staple of roadside cooking. Terrain: Grasslands, agricultural lowlands, forest edges Yield: 1 portion per bird (1d3 birds per successful hunt) Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Ayu (Sweetfish) A slender, silvery river fish prized for its clean, faintly melon-like flavor. Found in fast-flowing streams with gravel beds across Hana and Mizu. Traditionally grilled whole on skewers over charcoal — a sight at every summer festival and riverside stall. Terrain: Clear rivers, mountain streams, waterfall pools Yield: 1d4 fish per hour of fishing (1 portion per fish) Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Suzume (Sparrow) Tiny birds found everywhere — rooftops, rice fields, forest edges, temple eaves. More effort than meat, but skewered and grilled in batches they make a satisfying trail snack. Market stalls in Heian sell them five to a stick. Terrain: Universal — settlements, farmland, forest edges Yield: 1d4 birds per hour of trapping (3 birds = 1 portion) Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Tanishi (Paddy Snail) Dark-shelled freshwater snails found in rice paddies and slow-moving irrigation channels. The meat is small but flavorful when simmered in broth. Peasant food, looked down upon by the urban classes, but a reliable protein source for travelers passing through agricultural country. Terrain: Rice paddies, irrigation channels, lakeshores (Hana, Mizu, Tsuchi) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of gathering Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Yamadori (Copper Pheasant) A large, copper-plumed game bird found in the dense understory of lowland and hill forests. The meat is darker and more flavorful than quail, with enough substance for a proper meal. Wary and difficult to approach — more often snared than shot. Terrain: Hardwood forests, hillside brush, bamboo thickets Yield: 2 portions per bird Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Shika (Common Deer) The standard deer of Hokori's lowland forests and open hill country. Smaller than the sei-touched ryūjika, but far more common and easier to hunt. The venison is lean and clean-tasting, better fresh than preserved. Terrain: Lowland forests, open hillsides, forest margins (most provinces) Yield: 4–6 portions per deer Weight: 1 lb per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Funa (Crucian Carp) A hardy pond and slow-river fish with firm, slightly earthy flesh. Not prestigious — city cooks dismiss it as peasant food — but reliable and abundant. Farmers net them from irrigation ponds between seasons, and children learn to catch them with bent pins and reed line. Best when cleaned immediately and simmered in miso. Terrain: Ponds, rice-paddy overflow channels, slow rivers (Hana, Kusa, Tsuchi) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of fishing (1 portion per fish) Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Iwashi (Sardine) Small, oil-rich sea fish that run in enormous silver schools along the Nami and Mizu coasts. Caught in nets by the thousand during seasonal runs, then salted, dried, or grilled fresh the same day. The fat renders quickly over a fire and the flesh is intensely savoury. A cornerstone of coastal cuisine and a common sight on roadside grills inland during the runs. Terrain: Coastal waters, tidal shallows (Nami, Mizu) — seasonal runs Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of coastal fishing (2 fish per portion) Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Hato (Wild Dove) The broad-winged forest dove common to lowland Hana and the wooded margins of Kusa. Darker and more flavourful than quail, with enough meat on a single bird to make a proper meal. Often snared with rice bait or brought down with a staff-sling. A traveller's favourite because a dove in the pot is a full stomach by evening. Terrain: Lowland hardwood forest, forest edges, cultivated margins Yield: 1–2 portions per bird Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Uncommon

Kinuo (Gold-Tail Fish) The prized fish of the Kinryūgawa. Flesh is pale gold with a rich, buttery flavor. Runs heaviest in late spring and early autumn at the Sutariba's mouth near Natsumura. Commands premium prices in Heian — catching one in the wild is a stroke of fortune. Terrain: Kinryūgawa, Sutariba, Serenia-kai tributaries Yield: 2–3 portions per fish Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 5 sp

Inoshishi (Wild Boar) Muscular, dark-fleshed boar found in the forests of Hana, Kaze, and Kusa. Aggressive when cornered — hunting one is not a passive affair. The meat is dense and flavorful, best slow-cooked. Terrain: Dense forest, bamboo thickets, foothills Yield: 4–6 portions per boar Weight: 1 lb per portion | Cost: 3 cp

Yuki-kiji (Snow Pheasant) White-feathered game bird found at altitude in Sora and the upper Tenchūsan Ren. The meat is lean and slightly sweet. The feathers are prized for fletching. Terrain: Mountain passes above the cloud line, Hoshimori Plateau Yield: 1–2 portions per bird Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 1 sp

Iwana (Rock Char) A cold-water fish found in high mountain streams where the water runs fast and clear over stone. The flesh is firm, pink, and delicate — best eaten the same day it is caught. Prized by monks and mountain hermits who consider it the purest of all fish. Terrain: Mountain streams above 3,000 feet, waterfall basins (Sora, Tenchūsan Ren, Kaze highlands) Yield: 1–2 portions per fish Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 1 sp

Unagi (Freshwater Eel) Long, muscular eels found in river mud and estuary shallows. Catching one requires patience and a specific technique — they are slippery in every sense. The meat is rich, fatty, and deeply savory when grilled with a sweet soy glaze. Considered a stamina food across the archipelago. Terrain: River estuaries, muddy streambeds, lake shallows (Hana, Mizu, Kusa) Yield: 2–3 portions per eel Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 2 sp

Kamo (Wild Duck) Migratory ducks found on lakes, ponds, and the marshy edges of the Serenia-kai. Plentiful in autumn and winter. The meat is dark, rich, and gamey — a step above the common birds in both flavor and difficulty. Terrain: Lakes, marshland, coastal wetlands (seasonal — autumn through spring) Yield: 2–3 portions per bird Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 1 sp

Suppon (Softshell Turtle) Found in warm, slow-moving rivers and the thermal shallows of Hi province. The meat is lean and gelatinous, valued for soups. The shell is discarded, but the blood is sometimes mixed with sake as a tonic. Difficult to catch — they bite and do not let go. Terrain: Warm rivers, thermal pools, lake shallows (Hi, southern Hana) Yield: 3–4 portions per turtle Weight: 1 lb per portion | Cost: 3 sp

Taka-usagi (Highland Hare) A larger, tougher cousin of the mountain hare, found only above the cloud line in Sora and on the upper slopes of the Tenchūsan Ren. The fur is thick and silver-grey. The meat is darker, more flavorful, and holds up well in stews. Known for its wariness — tracking one is a test of patience. Terrain: High-altitude plateau, alpine grassland (Sora, upper Tenchūsan Ren) Yield: 2–3 portions per hare Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 1 sp

Rare

Seireiuo (Spirit Fish) Translucent freshwater fish found in sei-active waterways — the luminescent rivers of Kusa, the thermal streams of Hi, and rare pools deep in the Yōsei Mori. The flesh glows faintly for an hour after the fish is killed. The taste is clean and bright, almost floral. Terrain: Sei-active waterways, Yōsei Mori, thermal springs Yield: 1–2 portions per fish Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 2 gp

Ryūjika (Dragon Deer) A large, sei-touched deer species found in old-growth forests near Progenitor-associated sites. The antlers branch in patterns that resemble draconic script. The venison is extraordinarily rich and carries a faint warmth on the tongue even when served cold. Terrain: Ancient forests, Seidōrin Mori interior, near buried ruins Yield: 6–8 portions per deer Weight: 1 lb per portion | Cost: 5 gp

Oniuo (Demon Fish) A large, aggressive freshwater predator found in deep river pools and underground waterways. The body is covered in bony plates, the jaw is underslung, and the eyes reflect light like a cat's. The flesh is white, firm, and surprisingly mild — the difficulty is in the catching. An oniuo will fight a line for an hour and has been known to drag unwary fishermen into the water. Terrain: Deep river pools, underground waterways, Kagerō Gorge Yield: 4–6 portions per fish Weight: 1 lb per portion | Cost: 3 gp

Kumokiji (Cloud Pheasant) A large, iridescent game bird found only above the cloud line on the Hoshimori Plateau and the highest ridges of Sora province. The plumage shifts color with the light — silver to pale blue to white. The meat is tender, faintly sweet, and carries a clean, almost mineral quality. The birds are solitary and nearly silent, making them extraordinarily difficult to locate. Terrain: Hoshimori Plateau, highest ridgelines of Sora Yield: 2–3 portions per bird Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 4 gp

Kaseki-gani (Stone Crab) Enormous crabs found in tidal caves and submerged coastal caverns, particularly along Mizu's irregular coastline and the Tidal Caves of Umigakure. The shell is thick and mineral-encrusted, requiring tools to crack. The claw meat inside is dense, sweet, and extraordinarily rich — a single crab can feed a party. Terrain: Tidal caves, submerged coastal caverns, deep rock pools (Mizu, Nami) Yield: 4–6 portions per crab Weight: 1 lb per portion | Cost: 3 gp

Tsuchimogura (Earth Mole) A large, blind burrowing creature found in the deep soil of Tsuchi province and the lower slopes of Kurogane Yama. Not a true mole — closer in size to a badger, with powerful digging claws and dense, flavorful meat. Hunted by farmers who consider them pests but know their meat is excellent braised. Finding a burrow requires tracking the characteristic raised-earth trails. Terrain: Deep agricultural soil, forested slopes, river valleys (Tsuchi, southern Hana) Yield: 3–4 portions per creature Weight: 1 lb per portion | Cost: 2 gp

Kōri-iwana (Frost Char) A rare variant of the iwana found only in glacier-fed pools and the coldest mountain springs of Sora. The scales carry a faint blue iridescence and the flesh is so cold it numbs the tongue. Must be prepared quickly — the meat loses its distinctive character within hours of the catch. Terrain: Glacier-fed pools, ice-melt springs, highest mountain streams (Sora) Yield: 1–2 portions per fish Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 3 gp

Very Rare

Ryūgame (Dragon Turtle) A small, sei-touched turtle found in deep pools near Progenitor shrine sites. The shell bears natural patterns that echo draconic script. The meat is rich and gelatinous, and the broth made from the shell imparts a warmth that settles into the marrow. Hunting one feels transgressive — they are beautiful, ancient-seeming creatures. Many gatherers who find one choose to leave it be. Terrain: Deep pools near Progenitor shrines, sei-active lake beds Yield: 2–3 portions per turtle Weight: 1 lb per portion | Cost: 25 gp

Seirei-taka (Spirit Hawk) A sei-touched raptor found at extreme altitude on the Hoshimori Plateau, where the stars seem close enough to touch. The feathers glow faintly at night. The meat is lean and carries a sharp, electric quality on the tongue. These birds are sacred to the observatory communities of Sora — hunting one without their blessing is considered a grave offense. Even with permission, the hunt is extraordinarily difficult. Terrain: Hoshimori Plateau summit, highest peaks of Sora Yield: 1–2 portions per bird Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 50 gp

Kinryūgoi (Golden Dragon Carp) An enormous, gold-scaled carp found only in the deepest reaches of the Kinryūgawa during the autumn equinox. Local fishermen speak of them as legend — most have never seen one. The flesh is pale gold, rich beyond description, and carries a warmth that persists for hours after eating. The scales are valued by armorers and artisans. Terrain: Kinryūgawa deep pools, equinox only Yield: 6–8 portions per fish Weight: 1 lb per portion | Cost: 100 gp

One-Time Harvests

Some creatures yield cuts that will never again enter a cooking pot — named spirit-beasts, ancient mountain predators, things slain once in the memory of a generation. These harvests are recorded here as canon for tracking purposes, not as ingredients that can be gathered again. The quality of each yield reflects the butchering check on the day.

Yama-no-Ōkami (Mountain God of the Tenchūsan Ren)

Slain in the mountain pass during the Fushichō ashfall. A Huge-category beast — roughly twelve to fifteen feet from nose to haunch, eight feet at the shoulder, and weighing somewhere between six and eight thousand pounds. Butchered with exceptional skill — the natural 20 on the harvest check triggered the bonus d10 and cleared the Legendary threshold, securing every cut the beast had to offer, including the Reikokoro.

Ōkami-niku (Mountain God's Flesh) — Uncommon Dense, dark-grained muscle from the shoulders and haunches, marbled with winter fat and deeply flavoured from a lifetime of predation at altitude. The meat carries a faint mineral tang — cold stone and pine smoke — that no ordinary game possesses. Cooks well in almost any preparation, though the flavour is strong enough to overpower delicate seasonings. Source: Yama-no-Ōkami (one-time harvest) Yield: 8 portions Weight: 2 lb per portion | Cost: 3 gp per portion if sold | Keeps: 3 days fresh, indefinitely if smoked or salted

Ōkami no Abura (Mountain God's Rendered Fat) — Uncommon Thick layers of pale winter fat from beneath the hide, rendered down over a long fire into a clear, amber-gold tallow. A spoonful transforms any pan-fry — meat sears faster, vegetables crisp cleaner, and the aroma carries a distant suggestion of thunder. Keeps indefinitely if stored cold. Source: Yama-no-Ōkami subcutaneous fat (one-time harvest) Yield: 6 portions Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 2 gp per portion | Keeps: indefinitely

Shirokiba no Zui (White-Fang Marrow) — Rare Rich marrow drawn from the long bones of the forelimbs, pale as bleached bone and dense as cream. Roasted and spread on warm rice it produces an almost overwhelming umami. A cook with cook's utensils proficiency can split one portion across an entire party's meal. Source: Yama-no-Ōkami femurs and forelimbs (one-time harvest) Yield: 3 portions Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 8 gp per portion | Keeps: 4 days if kept cold

Yama no Kimo (Mountain Liver) — Rare A dark, fist-sized organ still faintly warm when pulled from the body cavity. Traditional mountain cooks consider this the single finest organ meat in Hokori — it carries a trace of the creature's essence, and eating it is said to sharpen the nerve and steady the breath. Suitable for a Refined dish. Source: Yama-no-Ōkami (one-time harvest) Yield: 2 portions Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 15 gp per portion | Keeps: 1 day fresh, 7 days salted or smoked

Arashi-suji (Storm-Sinew) — Rare Long tendons drawn from the legs and spine. Under the right light they carry a faint static shimmer — a residue of the creature's connection to the high mountain storms. Slow-braised into broth they impart a tension to the muscles of those who drink it, a wound-tight readiness that lingers into the following day. Suitable for a Refined dish. Source: Yama-no-Ōkami (one-time harvest) Yield: 3 portions Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 12 gp per portion | Keeps: 2 days fresh, 14 days dried

Reikokoro (Spirit Heart) — Legendary The creature's heart, roughly the size of a man's head and several times heavier, still faintly warm hours after death. Dense, dark red, and threaded with silver-white veins that pulsed once when first exposed to air before going still. It takes two grown men working together to lift it cleanly from the chest cavity, and one of them will need both hands. Mountain hunters speak of the reikokoro only in hushed terms — one portion, one meal, one chance. In the entire recorded history of Hokori's mountain provinces, a handful of cooks have been trusted with such an organ. None of them ever forgot the meal. Suitable for a Masterwork dish that feeds the entire party. Source: Yama-no-Ōkami (one-time harvest — unrepeatable) Yield: 1 portion (feeds up to six generously) Weight: 35 lb | Cost: Priceless — no established market; a shugo or temple abbot might offer 500+ gp for the honour of preparing it themselves | Keeps: 2 days fresh, indefinitely if salted

Non-Food Components

The exceptional harvest preserved more than just meat. The hide came off whole, the paws came clean, the great bones were salvaged before the carcass cooled, and the skull was lifted intact from the spine.

Ōkami no Kegawa (Mountain God's Pelt) A single enormous pelt taken from the back, flanks, and shoulders of the beast. The fur is silver-grey at the roots and deepens to charcoal at the tips, dense enough to turn a winter wind and long enough at the ruff that a man could bury both hands to the wrist in it. In low light the guard hairs catch a faint cool sheen — not luminous, but suggestive, the way frost catches starlight. Wolves are sacred animals in much of Hokori, and a pelt of this size and clarity is the kind of object that nobles, temple elders, and master leatherworkers will compete to acquire. Worked into a cloak it grants its wearer real status — and warmth that no ordinary fur can match. A seimaster might recognise it as a viable focus for ceremonial garments. Source: Yama-no-Ōkami (one-time harvest) Yield: 1 primary pelt (back and flanks) + 2 secondary sections (belly and limbs) Weight: 100 lb primary, 35 lb each secondary Value: 400–600 gp for the primary pelt raw; 1,200+ gp if commissioned into a finished cloak by a master leatherworker. Secondary sections: 80–120 gp each.

Ōkami no Tenohira (Mountain God's Paws) Four massive paws, each broader than a man's chest and heavy enough to need both hands to lift, removed cleanly at the wrist joint. The pads are thick black leather, deeply callused from a lifetime walking on stone, and the dew claws and main claws are intact and unbroken — a testament to the quality of the harvest. In Hokori folk tradition, the paw of a great wolf is hung above the door of a household to ward off mountain spirits and protect those within from being lost in the wilds. Bone-carvers and amulet-makers will pay well for whole paws, and a seimaster will pay better. The claws alone, if separated, fetch additional value as reagents and ornament. Source: Yama-no-Ōkami (one-time harvest) Yield: 4 intact paws (with claws and dew claws attached) Weight: 30 lb per paw Value: 80–120 gp per paw whole; 15–25 gp per individual claw if separated (5 claws per paw); higher if worked into a finished charm or ward

Ōkami no Hone (Mountain God's Bones) A clean butchering preserved the long bones of the legs, the heavy bones of the spine, and the great curved ribs. Bone of this size and density is genuinely uncommon — most predators in Hokori are smaller creatures whose bones snap rather than carve. A bone-carver can shape these into hilts, scabbard fittings, ornamental inlays, and the kind of polished accents that mark an expensive weapon or a noble's accessories. There is enough material here to keep a single craftsman supplied for years. Source: Yama-no-Ōkami (one-time harvest) Yield: ~350 lb of usable carving bone (long bones, ribs, vertebrae) Weight: 350 lb total — too much to carry whole; typically broken down and stored or sold by the lot Value: 5–8 gp per lb raw; 12–20 gp per lb cut and sized for craftsmen

Ōkami no Zugai (Mountain God's Skull) The skull was lifted intact from the spine — a fanged mask the size and shape of a temple bell, its great jaws still locked in their final snarl, the orbital sockets large enough that a child could put a fist into one. The bone is pale grey and unusually heavy, threaded with fine darker veining beneath the surface. As an object it is genuinely arresting — visitors to a hall containing such a skull tend to fall silent on first seeing it, and stay that way longer than is comfortable. Mountain temples have been known to enshrine such skulls when the slain creature was thought to be the avatar of a kami, and the priests of those temples will pay extraordinary sums — or refuse to pay anything at all and instead offer something else entirely. Source: Yama-no-Ōkami (one-time harvest) Yield: 1 intact skull Weight: 100 lb Value: 600–900 gp as a trophy piece on the open market; potentially priceless if offered to the right shrine, where the offering itself may be worth more than coin

Ōkami no Kiba (Mountain God's Fangs) The nat 20 harvest also yielded the long canine teeth clean and intact, drawn separately from the jaw before the skull was preserved. A bone-carver in any reasonably sized settlement will pay handsomely for worked fangs of this size, and a seimaster may recognise them as a viable reagent for a charm or focus. Source: Yama-no-Ōkami (one-time harvest) Yield: 4 intact fangs Weight: 2½ lb per fang Value: 40–60 gp per fang raw; higher if worked

Secret — Skill Check Knowledge

DM only. The full value of these components is not obvious. Players who succeed on the appropriate Religion, Nature, or Arcana check learn what their harvest is actually good for. A character may attempt one check per component per skill, with the check made when the component is first examined or when the character has reason to investigate it further. A natural 20 reveals everything across all three skills for that component.

Ōkami no Kegawa — Pelt

  • Religion (DC 13) — Wolves are sacred to many of the mountain kami, and a pelt of this clarity would be received as an extraordinary offering at any mountain shrine. A shrine receiving it would owe the giver a favour — the kind of favour that gets remembered for years. In Sora, Tsuchi, or upper Kaze, this could open doors that gold cannot.
  • Nature (DC 12) — The pelt is from a once-in-a-generation specimen. The character understands which sections are most valuable, how the hide must be cured, and that a master leatherworker (not a common one) is required to do the work properly. Identifies the leatherworkers of Heian, Kumo-no-Ue, and Akatsuki as having the requisite skill.
  • Arcana (DC 15) — The faint cool sheen in low light is real sei resonance — the creature's spiritual nature has imprinted on its fur. Worked into a ceremonial garment, the pelt could serve as an arcane focus for protection, divination, or ward-based magics. A seimaster who handles such a cloak would feel it.

Ōkami no Tenohira — Paws

  • Religion (DC 12) — The folk tradition of hanging a wolf paw above a household doorway is older than most temples — it predates the formal Shinto observances and is rooted in pre-imperial mountain beliefs. A paw mounted properly above a door is a genuine spiritual ward against being led astray in the wilds. Effective even for unbelievers.
  • Nature (DC 14) — The depth of callus on the pads tells the character that this creature walked exclusively on stone, not soft ground — confirming it lived its entire life in the high passes. The paws can be processed into trophy mounts, rugs, or grip-leather for weapon hilts. Identifies the proper preservation methods.
  • Arcana (DC 13) — The claws carry trace sei imprint and would serve as reagents for the crafting of protection charms, amulets against being lost, or low-level wards. Worth significantly more to a charm-maker than to a bone-carver.

Ōkami no Hone — Bones

  • Religion (DC 13) — Bones of a creature thought to be a kami avatar carry spiritual weight. Ground into bone meal and presented at a shrine, they constitute a significant offering. Carved into prayer beads or ritual implements, they serve as a permanent reminder of the offering and may carry the kami's favour with them.
  • Nature (DC 11) — Excellent carving stock. The character can identify which bones are best suited to which products — femurs for sword hilts, ribs for scabbard fittings, vertebrae for ornaments and beads. Knows the going rate per pound raw and per pound cut.
  • Arcana (DC 14) — The bone is resonant — it carries a faint sei echo when struck, a quality prized by arcane focus makers. Carved into a focus, it would suit a seimaster whose practice leans toward warding, banishment, or anti-spirit magics. Particularly valuable to seimasters in Sora and Kaze.

Ōkami no Zugai — Skull

  • Religion (DC 14) — The skull of a kami avatar is a relic. The mountain temples of Sora, upper Kaze, and Tsuchi maintain a tradition of enshrinement for such skulls — placing them in a sealed inner chamber, before which offerings are made for the spirit's onward journey. A temple receiving this skull would consider the giver to be marked by the kami in question, in a way that is generally considered fortunate but is occasionally not.
  • Nature (DC 12) — The wear on the teeth and the size of the orbital ridges suggest a creature in its prime, perhaps a century old. The character can read the diet from the molars (predominantly meat, but also some plant matter — unusual for a wolf) and identify the species characteristics that mark this as more than a normal beast.
  • Arcana (DC 16) — The skull retains a strong sei imprint — the strongest of any of the components. It could be turned into a ward-mask for ritual use, a powerful arcane focus, or a vessel for binding magics.
