A skilled seimaster could conceivably use it to commune with the creature's lingering essence, though doing so would risk drawing the attention of whatever kami the beast served in life. Detect Magic registers it clearly.

Ōkami no Kiba — Fangs

  • Religion (DC 11) — Long-standing tradition uses wolf fangs as protective charms, particularly for travellers crossing mountain passes. Hung from a cord at the throat or tied to a belt, a fang offers a small but real ward against being attacked by wild beasts.
  • Nature (DC 10) — Easily identified as adult predator canines in exceptional condition. Carving stock for amulets, daggerhilt accents, or ornamental inlays.
  • Arcana (DC 13) — Reagent for charm and focus crafting. Particularly suited to weapon enchantments — a fang set into the pommel of a blade can serve as a focus for spells that augment the weapon's bite.

Reikokoro — Spirit Heart

  • Religion (DC 15) — Eating the heart of a kami avatar is a profound act, and the tradition surrounding it is divided. Some mountain sects consider it transgressive — a violation of the spirit's onward journey. Others consider it sacred — a sharing of essence between the slain and the slayer. If the meal is prepared at a shrine with proper rites, the latter interpretation prevails, and the eaters may be marked by the kami's blessing for some time after.
  • Nature (DC 13) — The character recognizes the heart as exceptional spirit-flesh, understands that it must be cooked fresh or properly preserved, and knows that the preparation requires great care. Suggests cook's utensils proficiency at minimum.
  • Arcana (DC 16) — The heart retains a fragment of the creature's essence. A character with arcane training senses it on contact — a low, steady warmth like banked coals. Eating it grants more than ordinary nourishment; it transfers a small portion of the creature's spiritual nature to the eater. (DM: this is the mechanical justification for the Masterwork buff — the players don't need to know the mechanics, but a character who passes this check understands why the meal will matter.)

II. Herbs & Greens — Yakusō (薬草)

Common

Yamashiso (Mountain Perilla) Aromatic herb with broad purple-green leaves. Grows wild on hillsides and forest edges across most provinces. Used fresh as a garnish, dried as a seasoning, or steeped as a tea. Mildly stimulating. Terrain: Hillsides, forest edges, roadsides (all provinces) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Seri (Water Parsley) Crisp, peppery herb found along streams and in wet meadows. One of the first wild greens to appear in spring. A common addition to soups and rice dishes throughout the countryside. Terrain: Streamsides, wet meadows, rice paddy edges Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Nobiru (Wild Garlic) Slender bulbs with a sharp, clean bite. Found in open grasslands and along the Emperor's Highway margins. Often eaten raw or pickled. The smell deters certain insects. Terrain: Grasslands, roadsides, open hillsides Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Yomogi (Mugwort) A tough, aromatic herb with silvery-green leaves found along roadsides and disturbed ground throughout Hokori. Bitter when raw, but blanched and pounded into rice cakes it produces the distinctive green kusamochi sold at every festival. Also burned as a smudge to repel insects at camp. Terrain: Roadsides, field margins, disturbed ground (all provinces) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Warabi (Bracken Fern) Young fiddlehead ferns harvested in spring from forest floors and hillsides. Must be soaked overnight in wood ash water to remove bitterness before eating. A staple wild green across the archipelago — gathering warabi is one of the first foraging skills children learn. Terrain: Forest floors, shaded hillsides, bamboo grove margins (most provinces) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Mitsuba (Trefoil) A delicate, three-leafed herb with a bright, celery-like flavor. Grows in shaded, damp areas near streams and under forest canopy. Used as a garnish in soups and custards, or scattered over rice. The flavor is subtle but distinctive — it marks the difference between trail cooking and something worth eating. Terrain: Shaded streamsides, forest understory, temple garden margins Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Takenoko (Bamboo Shoot) Young bamboo shoots harvested in spring from the edges of bamboo groves. Must be boiled to remove bitterness. The tender inner flesh is crisp, mildly sweet, and absorbs flavor from whatever it is cooked with. Abundant where bamboo grows — which is most of lowland Hokori. Terrain: Bamboo groves, forest edges (Hana, Kusa, Mizu, Tsuchi) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging (spring only; 1d2 in other seasons) Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Shungiku (Chrysanthemum Greens) The edible leaves of wild chrysanthemum, with a distinctive aromatic bitterness that cuts through rich broths. Found in open sunny areas and along cultivated field margins. A common hot pot ingredient that also serves as a mild digestive aid. Terrain: Open fields, sunny hillsides, cultivated margins (most provinces) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Fuki (Butterbur) A tall, broad-leafed plant with thick, celery-like stalks that push up through the snow in early spring. The stalks are peeled, blanched, and simmered to remove a lingering bitterness — but the reward is a clean, fresh flavour that announces the end of winter. A beloved sign of the turning year in every mountain village. Terrain: Streamsides, damp meadows, shaded valleys (all provinces; spring peak) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Zenmai (Royal Fern) Tightly curled young fern heads, densely furred with golden down, harvested from the forest floor in spring. The down must be scrubbed off and the stalks soaked overnight before cooking. Once prepared they are meaty and faintly nutty, excellent in simmered dishes or dressed with miso. Mountain villagers preserve bundles of dried zenmai for winter cooking. Terrain: Forest floors, shaded hillsides, above spring snowmelt (mountain provinces) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging (spring only) Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Karashi-na (Mustard Greens) Broad, deep-green leaves with a sharp, peppery bite that mellows with cooking. Self-seeds along cultivated field margins and disturbed ground, especially in Tsuchi and Hana where farmers allow them to grow wild between plantings. Used in pickles, stir-fries, and the spicy soups of winter. Terrain: Field margins, disturbed ground, roadsides (Tsuchi, Hana, Kusa) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Uncommon

Kurokaze-sō (Black Wind Herb) A dark-leafed herb found only in Kaze province, growing in the shadow of black pines where the mist never fully lifts. Used by Gekkō-trained herbalists for alertness tinctures. Bitter, with a sharp aftertaste that clears the head. Terrain: Kaze province — black pine forests, mist-shrouded valleys Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 5 sp

Hi no Ha (Fire Leaf) A low-growing succulent with reddish-orange leaves, found near fumaroles and thermal vents in Hi province. The leaves produce a tingling heat when chewed, stronger than any cultivated pepper. Used sparingly in cooking — too much causes painful numbness. Terrain: Hi province — fumarole fields, volcanic slopes, near Honōgawa Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 3 sp

Tsukimisō (Moon-Viewing Herb) Pale silver flowers that open only at night, found on high ground in Sora and along ridgelines in Hana's mountains. The petals, dried and crumbled, produce a mild calming effect. Traditionally served in tea before important negotiations. Terrain: High-altitude ridgelines, Sora province, Tenchūsan Ren Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging (night only) Weight: — per portion | Cost: 5 sp

Umikaze-na (Sea Wind Greens) A thick-leafed coastal plant that grows on cliff faces and rocky shorelines where the salt spray is constant. The leaves are succulent, salty, and faintly bitter — eaten raw they taste of the sea. Nami fishermen chew them during long watches. Used in cooking to add a briny depth without additional salt. Terrain: Coastal cliffs, rocky shorelines, sea-spray zone (Nami, Mizu) Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 2 sp

Kagerō-sō (Shimmer Herb) A low, ground-hugging herb found along the banks of the Kagerō River in Kaze province, identifiable by the faint shimmer on its leaves that mirrors the river's thermal haze. The leaves have a complex, slightly numbing quality that enhances other flavors when used in small amounts. Overuse deadens the palate. Terrain: Kagerō River banks, thermal stream margins (Kaze) Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 3 sp

Iwa-ninniku (Cliff Garlic) A pungent wild garlic variant that grows from cracks in cliff faces and exposed rock. Stronger than lowland nobiru — the flavor is sharp, almost medicinal, and lingers for hours. Mountain villagers in Sora use it as both seasoning and folk remedy. Harvesting requires climbing or reaching into awkward crevices. Terrain: Cliff faces, exposed rock, mountain road cuttings (Sora, Tenchūsan Ren) Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 2 sp

Murasaki-ha (Purple Leaf) A broad-leafed plant endemic to Kusa's lowland forests, where it grows in the violet grass meadows alongside the native murasaki-gusa. The leaves are a deep purple-black and have a mild, earthy sweetness that complements rich meats. Kusa cooks wrap fish and game in the leaves before steaming — a regional technique unknown outside the province. Terrain: Kusa province — violet grasslands, lowland forest clearings Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 2 sp

Tsuchi-shōga (Earth Ginger) A knotty root found in the mineral-rich soil of Tsuchi province's agricultural valleys. Smaller and more intensely flavored than cultivated ginger, with a sharp heat and an earthy undertone that reflects the volcanic soil it grows in. Farmers dig it up as a byproduct of plowing and sell it at local markets. Terrain: Agricultural valleys, freshly turned soil (Tsuchi, southern Hana) Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging (1 root = 2 portions) Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 3 sp

Rare

Seiryoku-gusa (Sei-Vigor Grass) A luminous blue-green grass that grows in tight spirals near leyline concentrations and sei-active springs. The blades pulse with faint light when cut, and carry that glow for days after being dried. Herbalists in Sora and Kaze prize it for both cooking and minor focusing rituals. Terrain: Sei-active sites — Yōsei Mori, shrine surrounds, Whispering Flats Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 15 gp

Ryūketsu-bana (Dragon's Blood Flower) Deep crimson flower with gold-veined petals, found growing from cracks in stone near Progenitor-associated ruins. Blooms are small — no larger than a thumbnail — and extremely difficult to spot. The dried petals impart a metallic warmth to any dish. Terrain: Progenitor ruins, Seidōrin Mori deep interior, volcanic ridgelines Yield: 1 portion per successful forage Weight: — per portion | Cost: 10 gp

Ginrei-sō (Silver Spirit Herb) A frost-white herb that grows at extreme altitude on the Hoshimori Plateau, where it clings to rock faces in thin soil that freezes solid every night. The leaves are tough and fibrous — useless raw — but when simmered they release a clean, piercingly bright flavor that clears the sinuses and sharpens the mind. Sora's observatory seimasters brew it as a study aid. Terrain: Hoshimori Plateau rock faces, highest ridgelines of Sora Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 5 gp

Akabana (Crimson Bloom) A heat-loving flower found growing in volcanic ash near active vents in Hi province. The petals are a vivid crimson that deepens to black at the edges. When dried and crumbled into food, they produce a slow, building warmth that starts in the chest and spreads to the extremities. Hi province healers use them to treat exposure and hypothermia. Terrain: Active volcanic ash fields, fumarole margins (Hi province) Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 5 gp

Yūrei-kusa (Ghost Grass) A pale, almost transparent grass that grows in the shadow of ancient ruins and abandoned settlements — particularly around Tsukikage in Kaze province. It sways without wind and is cold to the touch even in summer. When brewed as a tea, it produces a heightened awareness of one's surroundings that borders on unsettling. Some drinkers report hearing whispers. Terrain: Abandoned settlements, ruined foundations, spirit-touched ground (Kaze, areas near Yurei) Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 8 gp

Mizuchi-na (Water Dragon Greens) A deep-green aquatic plant found in the clearest, coldest springs fed by snowmelt from the Tenchūsan Ren. The fronds are long and ribbon-like, and when held up to light they show veining that resembles scales. The flavor is bright, clean, and faintly metallic — like drinking from a mountain spring. Must be harvested underwater. Terrain: Cold mountain springs, snowmelt-fed pools (Tenchūsan Ren, Sora, upper Kaze) Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 5 gp

Kasumi-sō (Mist Herb) Found only in the dense fog banks of Kaze province's deepest valleys, where visibility drops to arm's length and sound arrives from the wrong direction. The herb is identifiable by scent alone — a sharp, green fragrance that cuts through the ambient dampness. Used in cooking, it produces a heightened clarity of taste in other ingredients, as though the fog around one's senses had been lifted. Terrain: Kaze province — perpetual fog zones, deep valley floors Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 7 gp

Very Rare

Ryūsō (Dragon Herb) A small, leathery-leafed plant found growing directly on the stone of Progenitor shrine sites, its roots apparently drawing sustenance from the rock itself. The leaves are warm to the touch year-round and carry a faint metallic sheen. When consumed, the flavor changes depending on the shrine's associated Progenitor — fiery near Crimson sites, cool and bright near Azure. Cannot be cultivated; attempts to transplant it kill the plant within hours. Terrain: Progenitor shrine sites only Yield: 1 portion per successful forage Weight: — per portion | Cost: not sold

Hoshikusa (Star Grass) A luminescent grass found only on the Hoshimori Plateau during specific celestial alignments — when Ryūgetsu enters full phase and the aurora of Hikarishō touches the ground. The blades glow with a shifting, opalescent light and are warm to the touch. The window for harvesting is narrow — hours at most. When used in cooking, it imparts a sensation that defies description: a warmth that feels like being watched over. Terrain: Hoshimori Plateau — during Hikarishō alignment only Yield: 1 portion per successful forage Weight: — per portion | Cost: not sold

Kaminari-kusa (Thunder Herb) Found only during active thunderstorms on exposed ridgelines — the herb appears to sprout from bare rock in the minutes following a lightning strike and withers within the hour. The leaves crackle faintly when touched and carry a sharp, ozone-like scent. Harvesting requires being on an exposed ridgeline during a thunderstorm, which is exactly as dangerous as it sounds. Terrain: Exposed ridgelines during thunderstorms (any mountain province) Yield: 1 portion per successful forage (if you survive the storm) Weight: — per portion | Cost: not sold

III. Fungi — Kinoko (茸)

Common

Shiitake (Oak Mushroom) The universal cooking mushroom of Kagekuni. Found on fallen hardwood throughout Hana, Kusa, and Mizu. Rich umami flavor. Dries well and keeps indefinitely. Terrain: Hardwood forests (most provinces) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Nameko (Amber Cap) Small, glossy mushrooms found in clusters on decaying wood in damp forests. Mild, slightly nutty. Common in soups and stews. Terrain: Damp forests, river valleys, cave mouths Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Shimeji (Beech Cluster) Clusters of small, round-capped mushrooms found at the base of beech and other broadleaf trees. The flavor is mild with a faint sweetness that develops when cooked. Plentiful enough that even an inexperienced forager can find them on a good day. Terrain: Broadleaf forests, beech groves, forest edges (Hana, Kusa, Mizu) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Kikurage (Wood Ear) Thin, translucent, ear-shaped fungi found on dead elder and willow wood near streams. The texture is crunchy and gelatinous — they contribute body rather than flavor. Widely used in soups and stir-fried dishes across all provinces. Dries flat and reconstitutes easily. Terrain: Streamside deadwood, willow groves, damp forest margins Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Hiratake (Oyster Shelf) Fan-shaped mushrooms growing in overlapping shelves on standing dead trees and fallen logs. The flesh is thick, meaty, and absorbs seasoning readily. A favorite of trail cooks because of its substantial texture — it can stand in for meat in lean times. Terrain: Standing deadwood, fallen logs, forest clearings (most provinces) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Matsutake (Pine Mushroom) Large, thick-stemmed mushrooms found under red pine trees in well-drained soil. The aroma is distinctive — a spicy, almost cinnamon-like fragrance that announces a find before you see it. Highly prized and seasonal — autumn only. Despite the prestige, they are common enough in the right terrain to be found by a patient forager. Terrain: Red pine forests, well-drained hillsides (Hana, Kaze, Kusa) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging (autumn only) Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 5 cp

Eringi (King Trumpet) Tall, thick-stemmed mushrooms found on dead roots and buried wood in grasslands and field margins. The cap is small relative to the meaty stem, which is the prized part — firm, white, and holds its texture through long cooking. Farmers in Tsuchi gather them from freshly cleared fields. Terrain: Grasslands, field margins, disturbed soil (Tsuchi, Kusa, Hana lowlands) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Maitake (Hen of the Woods) Large, ruffled clusters found at the base of old oak and chestnut trees, growing in tiered layers that can weigh several pounds each. The flavour is earthy and deep with a subtle peppery finish. Prized in autumn cooking — a single find can feed a party twice over and the dried trimmings keep well on the road. Considered a lucky discovery by foragers. Terrain: Base of mature oaks, chestnut groves, old-growth hardwood forests (Hana, Kusa, Kaze lowlands) — autumn peak Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging (1 find = 2–3 portions) Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Sugihiratake (Cedar Shelf) Pale, fan-shaped mushrooms that grow in dense overlapping shelves on fallen cedar and cypress logs in mountain forests. The flesh is thin but flavourful, with a distinctive resinous note from the wood beneath. Mountain villagers in Sora and Kaze gather them in bulk during damp autumns and dry them in strings beneath the eaves. Terrain: Fallen cedar and cypress, mountain forest deadwood (Sora, Kaze, Tenchūsan Ren foothills) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Haratake (Meadow Cap) Round, white-capped mushrooms found in open grasslands and grazed meadows, particularly where horses or cattle have passed. They push up in rings overnight after rain. The flavour is mild and slightly sweet — the most forgiving mushroom for new foragers, but also the easiest to mistake for dangerous lookalikes. Experienced gatherers teach children the telltale pink-to-brown gill colour. Terrain: Open grasslands, grazed meadows, fallow fields (Kusa, Tsuchi, Hana lowlands) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging (best in the hours after rain) Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Uncommon

Kageboushi (Shadow Cap) Found only in perpetually dark environments — deep caves, the interior of the Hollow Peaks, the lightless galleries beneath mountain temples. Caps are charcoal-black with a silvery underside. The flavor is deep and earthy, almost smoky. Terrain: Caves, underground passages, Kaze province deep forest Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 2 sp

Enokidake (Golden Thread Mushroom) Thin, pale mushrooms growing in dense clusters on decaying bronze-bark wood in the Seidōrin Mori. The metallic substrate gives them a faint coppery note. Highly prized by Heian chefs. Terrain: Seidōrin Mori (Bronze Wood Forest) Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 5 sp

Iwatake (Rock Mushroom) A flat, lichen-like fungus found clinging to cliff faces and exposed rock in mountain provinces. The texture is leathery when dried and gelatinous when rehydrated. The flavor is intensely mineral — almost metallic — and complements rich soups and braised dishes. Harvesting requires climbing or reaching into exposed positions. Terrain: Cliff faces, exposed mountain rock (Sora, Tenchūsan Ren, Kaze highlands) Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 3 sp

Kurenai-take (Crimson Cap) A brilliant red-capped mushroom found near hot springs and thermal vents in Hi province. Easily mistaken for a poisonous variety — only those who know the distinguishing underside pattern (pale gold gills rather than white) should pick them. The flavor is rich, almost smoky, with a warmth that reflects its volcanic habitat. Terrain: Hot spring margins, thermal vents, warm-soil areas (Hi province) Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 3 sp

Yuki-shimeji (Snow Cluster) A cold-hardy variant of the common shimeji found only above the snow line in Sora and on the highest ridges of the Tenchūsan Ren. The caps are pale blue-white and the stems are unusually crisp. The flavor is clean and slightly sweet, with a brightness that ordinary shimeji lack. Terrain: Above snow line, high altitude clearings (Sora, upper Tenchūsan Ren) Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 2 sp

Tanuki-take (Tanuki Mushroom) A squat, round-bodied mushroom with a mottled brown cap found in deciduous forests across Kusa and Hana. Named for its resemblance to a sleeping tanuki curled into a ball. The flesh is dense, almost meaty, with a rich umami that intensifies when dried. Forest communities in Kusa preserve them in great quantities for winter stores. Terrain: Deciduous forests, leaf litter, fallen broadleaf logs (Kusa, Hana) Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 2 sp

Shio-take (Salt Stalk) A pale, crystalline-crusted mushroom found in coastal caves where seawater seeps through limestone. The natural salt crust makes it unique — it serves as both ingredient and seasoning simultaneously. Nami fishermen use them in chowder-like stews where the salt dissolves into the broth. Terrain: Coastal limestone caves, sea-spray grottoes (Nami, Mizu) Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 3 sp

Rare

Seikinoko (Sei Mushroom) Luminescent mushrooms found deep within the Yōsei Mori and in caverns with active sei flow. They glow a soft violet-blue and the caps are warm to the touch. The taste is subtle — like forest air after rain — but the sei resonance within them is unmistakable. Terrain: Yōsei Mori interior, sei-active caverns, near spirit shrines Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 12 gp

Hinotake (Fire Stalk) Bright orange mushrooms that grow near volcanic vents in Hi province. The flesh is dry and slightly spicy. They thrive in temperatures that would kill any other fungus, drawing nutrients from volcanic mineral deposits. Must be handled carefully — the raw caps cause mild chemical burns on bare skin. Terrain: Hi province — volcanic vents, obsidian fields, thermal caves Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 5 gp

Tsukiyo-take (Moonlit Cap) A pale, luminescent mushroom found on deadwood in high-altitude forests during nights when Kagetsu is full. The cap glows with a soft silver light that fades within hours of picking. The flavor is elusive — dreamlike is the word most often used, though no one can articulate what that means. Some who eat them report unusually vivid dreams during the following rest. Terrain: High-altitude deadwood, open to moonlight (Sora, upper Kaze) — full Kagetsu only Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 8 gp

Kōtetsu-take (Steel Cap) A dark, metallic-capped mushroom found in the iron-rich soil around Kurogane Yama and the mining settlements of Tsuchi. The cap has a genuine metallic sheen and the flesh contains trace minerals that give it a faintly ferrous taste. Miners consider them good luck. Alchemists value them for the mineral content. Terrain: Iron-rich soil, mine tailings, Kurogane Yama slopes (Tsuchi) Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 4 gp

Arashi-take (Storm Cap) Found only on exposed surfaces after severe storms — typically on shattered tree trunks or freshly exposed rock faces in Nami province. The caps appear within hours of a major storm and wither within a day. They are electric blue with branching white patterns on the cap that resemble lightning. The flavor is sharp, almost astringent, with a tingling quality on the tongue. Terrain: Storm-damaged surfaces, exposed wood and rock (Nami, exposed coastline) — post-storm only Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 6 gp

Dokuro-take (Skull Cap) A bone-white mushroom found growing on ancient remains — specifically on buried skeletal material in battlefields, old gravesites, and ruined settlements. The cap is smooth and rounded, unsettlingly skull-like. Despite its morbid habitat, the flavor is mild and pleasant. Herbalists in Kaze province use it as a base for medicines that ease pain and promote rest. Terrain: Old battlefields, gravesites, ruined foundations with buried remains Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 5 gp

Kaseki-take (Fossil Shelf) A large, shelf-like fungus found growing on petrified wood in ancient geological formations — the Buried Road of Tsuchi, the deep foundations of Progenitor ruins, and exposed strata in river gorges. The flesh is incredibly dense and must be thinly sliced. The flavor is deep, complex, and ancient-tasting in a way that is difficult to articulate — like stone dust and old libraries and deep time. Terrain: Petrified wood, ancient geological formations, Buried Road (Tsuchi) Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of foraging Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 7 gp

Very Rare

Ryūkinoko (Dragon Fungus) A large, golden-capped mushroom found only in caverns directly beneath Progenitor resting sites. The cap is warm to the touch and radiates a faint light in darkness. The flesh carries a flavor that shifts with each bite — savory, then sweet, then something that sits between warmth and music. Those who eat it describe a sensation of profound calm. Terrain: Progenitor caverns, directly beneath dragon resting sites Yield: 1 portion per successful forage Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 50 gp

Hoshi-take (Star Cap) A tiny, brilliantly luminescent mushroom found on the Hoshimori Plateau during specific stellar alignments. The caps are no larger than a thumbnail and glow with a light that shifts through the spectrum — gold, blue, red, violet — mirroring the three-star system overhead. They appear in clusters and vanish by dawn. The taste is indescribable. Seimasters at Hoshimori have attempted to study them for decades without satisfactory results. Terrain: Hoshimori Plateau — during rare triple-star alignment only Yield: 1 portion per successful forage Weight: — per portion | Cost: not sold

Yomi-take (Underworld Cap) A pitch-black mushroom found in the deepest accessible caverns of Kagekuni — places where no light has reached in geological time. The cap absorbs light rather than reflecting it, creating a visual absence that is disorienting to look at directly. The flavor is the densest umami imaginable — concentrated essence of earth and darkness. Herbalists and seimasters debate whether it should be classified as a fungus at all. Terrain: Deepest caverns, places of absolute darkness, far beneath mountain roots Yield: 1 portion per successful forage Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: not sold

IV. Seasonings & Aromatics — Chōmiryō (調味料)

Common

Shio (Sea Salt) Harvested from evaporation pools along the Nami and Mizu coasts, or traded inland along the Emperor's Highway. The fundamental seasoning of Kagekuni cooking. Terrain: Coastal (purchased or harvested from tidal pools) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of harvesting (coastal only); unlimited when purchased Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Shōyu (Soy Paste) A fermented seasoning carried by most travelers and available in any settlement with a market. Not foraged — purchased or traded. Availability: Any settlement with commerce Yield: Purchased — not foraged Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Wasabi (Mountain Horseradish) Found wild along cool, shaded streams in the mountains. The root is grated fresh for a sharp, sinus-clearing heat. Cultivated near Ayame and in Kaze's valleys. Terrain: Mountain streams, shaded valleys Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging (1 root = 2 portions) Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Sanshō (Mountain Pepper) Small, citrus-scented peppercorns found on prickly shrubs along mountain trails and forest edges. The flavor is bright and tingling rather than hot — a numbing, almost electric sensation on the tongue. Used whole, cracked, or ground. Available nearly everywhere mountains meet forest. Terrain: Mountain trails, forest edges, shrubby hillsides (most provinces) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Myōga (Wild Ginger Bud) Pale pink buds found at the base of wild ginger plants in shaded, damp forest understory. The flavor is bright and peppery with a floral sharpness — sliced thin, it brightens any dish. Abundant in the right conditions but easy to overlook under leaf litter. Terrain: Shaded forest understory, damp leaf litter (Hana, Kusa, Mizu) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Kombu (Kelp) Broad, dark sheets of dried seaweed harvested from coastal rocks and tidal zones. The foundation of dashi stock. Available fresh along any coastline or dried in any market settlement. The umami it imparts to broth is irreplaceable. Terrain: Coastal rocks, tidal zones (Nami, Mizu); purchased dried elsewhere Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of harvesting (coastal only); unlimited when purchased Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Goma (Wild Sesame) Tiny seeds from a tall, flowering plant found in dry, open fields and along road margins. Toasted, they release a deep, nutty aroma that elevates simple rice dishes. The oil pressed from the seeds is used for frying and finishing. A common roadside find in the agricultural provinces. Terrain: Dry fields, road margins, sunny hillsides (Tsuchi, Hana, Kusa) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Yuzu (Mountain Citrus) A small, intensely aromatic citrus fruit found wild on thorny trees in hill forests and mountain slopes. The fruit itself is too sour to eat, but the zest and juice transform cooking — a few drops of yuzu juice in a broth is the difference between adequate and transcendent. Ripens in autumn. Terrain: Hill forests, mountain slopes, forest edges (Hana, Kaze, Sora foothills) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging (1 fruit = 2 portions; autumn peak) Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Tōgarashi (Hill Chili) Slender red peppers that grow on low shrubs along sun-warmed hillsides and field margins. Dried whole and crushed into flakes, or ground fine and blended with other spices. The heat is clean and bright rather than smouldering. Essential to the everyday cooking of Hi province and beloved everywhere the cold reaches in. Terrain: Sunny hillsides, field margins, cultivated land (Hi, Kusa, Hana; autumn harvest) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging (1 pod = 2 portions) Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Tade (Water Pepper) A slender, reed-edge herb whose leaves carry a sharp peppery bite — the wild cousin of cultivated spices. Fishermen along the Kinryūgawa use it as a traditional accompaniment to grilled river fish, and its leaves are often pressed onto sashimi as a pungent garnish. Abundant where clear water meets soft mud. Terrain: Riverbanks, stream margins, rice paddy edges (Hana, Kusa, Mizu) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Shiso-mi (Perilla Seeds) The dark, peppery seeds produced by mature perilla plants at the end of summer. Gathered by shaking ripe stalks over a cloth, then dried and cracked between the teeth or ground into a finishing dust. Adds a complex, almost medicinal depth to rice, fish, and pickles. Often mixed with salt for travel. Terrain: Hillsides, forest edges, cultivated margins (all provinces; late summer) Yield: 1d4 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Uncommon

Seidōrin no Shio (Bronze Wood Salt) Mineral salt collected from crystalline deposits at the base of bronze-barked trees in the Seidōrin Mori. Has a faintly metallic, almost sweet quality that enhances the flavor of game meats. Collection requires a clan license — unlicensed harvesting is technically a capital offense. Terrain: Seidōrin Mori (licensed access only) Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of harvesting Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 5 sp

Kuro-koshō (Black Mountain Pepper) Found in the underbrush of Kaze's black pine forests. Berries are tiny, dark, and intensely aromatic — cracked between the teeth, they release a complex heat that builds slowly and lingers. Kaze merchants sell them at a premium. Terrain: Kaze province — black pine forest understory Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 5 sp

Kaen-su (Flame Vinegar) A pungent vinegar produced naturally in thermal pools of Hi province where specific mineral concentrations and bacterial colonies create an acidic brine. The liquid is collected from shallow depressions near volcanic vents — it tastes of heat, stone, and a sharp acidity that cuts through the richest meat. Cannot be replicated outside its volcanic source. Terrain: Thermal pool margins, volcanic mineral deposits (Hi province) Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of harvesting Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 3 sp

Umi-shio (Deep Sea Salt) Coarse, grey-blue salt crystals harvested from deep tidal caves along Nami's coastline, where centuries of seawater evaporation have left mineral-rich deposits on cave walls. The flavor is more complex than ordinary sea salt — briny, faintly bitter, with a mineral depth that ordinary salt lacks. Nami fishermen consider it essential for proper fish curing. Terrain: Deep tidal caves, cave walls above high-water mark (Nami coastline) Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of harvesting Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 3 sp

Tsuchi-miso (Earth Miso) A wild fermented paste found in clay deposits near certain hot springs in Hi and Tsuchi provinces, where soil bacteria and mineral content produce a natural fermentation in accumulated organic matter. The result is a dark, intensely savory paste — rougher than manufactured miso, but with a depth that cultured products cannot match. Not all deposits are safe to eat — local knowledge is essential. Terrain: Hot spring clay deposits, mineral-rich soil (Hi, Tsuchi) — requires local guidance Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of harvesting Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 4 sp

Kumo-no-Su Kōji (Cloud Nest Mold) A beneficial mold culture found growing on grain stores in the high-altitude settlements of Sora, where the cold, dry air and altitude produce unique fermentation conditions. The mold is collected and used to inoculate rice for a distinctively sharp, clean sake and a fermented seasoning paste with an almost effervescent quality. The communities of Kumo-no-Ue guard their specific culture strains carefully. Terrain: High-altitude grain stores (Sora province — Kumo-no-Ue, Hoshimori) Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of careful collection Weight: — per portion | Cost: 5 sp

Nami no Hana (Wave Blossom) A dried sea foam that crystallizes on coastal rocks during the height of Tatsunami season, when the four-moon alignment drives extreme tides. The crystals are white, feathery, and dissolve on the tongue with an intense brininess followed by an unexpected sweetness. Used as a finishing salt on delicate dishes. Available only during a narrow seasonal window. Terrain: Exposed coastal rocks during Tatsunami (Nami, Mizu coastline) — seasonal Yield: 1d3 portions per hour of harvesting Weight: — per portion | Cost: 5 sp

Rare

Ryūjio (Dragon Salt) Crystalline mineral deposits found in caverns near Progenitor-associated sites. The crystals are warm to the touch and dissolve slowly, releasing a flavor that shifts — first savory, then faintly sweet, then something that has no earthly comparison. A single pinch transforms a dish. Terrain: Progenitor-associated caverns, deep ruins Yield: 1d2 portions per successful forage Weight: — per portion | Cost: 15 gp

Kuroyō-su (Obsidian Vinegar) A naturally occurring acidic mineral brine found seeping through obsidian formations in the Kuroso fields of Hi province. The liquid is dark, almost black, and carries a sharp acidity with an underlying smokiness. Alchemists use it as a reagent; cooks use it — very sparingly — as a finishing acid that adds complexity no other vinegar can match. Terrain: Obsidian Fields of Kurosō, volcanic glass formations (Hi province) Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of careful collection Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 8 gp

Seidō-kōji (Bronze Mold) A rare fermentation culture found on fallen bronze-bark in the deepest, dampest reaches of the Seidōrin Mori. The mold itself is a pale green-gold and imparts a unique metallic complexity to whatever it ferments. Used to produce a seasoning paste of extraordinary depth — savory, faintly sweet, with a lingering copper brightness. Harvesting requires entering restricted forest areas. Terrain: Deep Seidōrin Mori, fallen bronze-bark in damp hollows Yield: 1d2 portions per successful forage Weight: — per portion | Cost: 10 gp

Rei-en (Spirit Salt) Crystalline deposits found at the margins of sei-active springs and pools, where the interaction between sei energy and mineral-rich water produces salt crystals that are faintly warm and carry a subtle luminescence. The flavor is clean and bright — not quite salt, not quite sweet, but something adjacent to both. Dissolves instantly on contact with food. Terrain: Sei-active springs, luminescent pool margins (Yōsei Mori, shrine pools) Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of careful collection Weight: — per portion | Cost: 15 gp

Kazan-koshō (Volcano Pepper) The fruit of a stunted bush that grows in the ash fields surrounding Enshiyama's crater, where soil temperatures remain elevated year-round. The berries are tiny and dark red, and the heat they carry is unlike any other pepper — it builds slowly, reaches an almost painful intensity, then subsides into a deep, smoky warmth. Hi province alchemists classify it as mildly toxic. Hi province cooks classify anyone who can't handle it as weak. Terrain: Enshiyama ash fields, volcanic crater margins (Hi province) Yield: 1d2 portions per hour of foraging Weight: — per portion | Cost: 6 gp

Gin-en (Silver Salt) Pale, almost transparent crystal deposits found in caverns near the Silver Dragon's associated sites. The crystals are cold to the touch regardless of ambient temperature and dissolve with a clean, bright flavor followed by a cooling sensation that lingers. Used in dishes meant to counteract heat or fever, or simply as a finishing seasoning of extraordinary refinement. Terrain: Caverns near Ginryū-associated sites, high-altitude mineral deposits Yield: 1d2 portions per successful forage Weight: — per portion | Cost: 12 gp

Yūgure-su (Twilight Vinegar) A deep amber liquid that collects in hollows of ancient hardwood trees in the Yōsei Mori, where sei activity and slow fermentation of tree sap produce a vinegar of remarkable complexity. The flavor carries notes of autumn leaves, honey, and something that suggests distance — like a memory of a taste rather than the taste itself. The trees that produce it are centuries old and cannot be cultivated. Terrain: Ancient hardwood hollows, Yōsei Mori interior Yield: 1d2 portions per successful forage Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 10 gp

Very Rare

Ryū no Namida (Dragon's Tear) A liquid mineral seep found in the deepest chambers of Progenitor-associated cave systems — slow drops that fall from stone ceilings into shallow basins over decades. The liquid is perfectly clear, faintly warm, and carries no scent. On the tongue it produces a sensation of pure, complex flavor that defies categorization — every person who tastes it describes something different. A single drop can transform an entire dish. The basins are found near places where Progenitors rested. Terrain: Deepest Progenitor cavern chambers, dragon resting sites Yield: 1 portion per successful forage Weight: — per portion | Cost: not sold

Hoshi no Kona (Star Dust) A fine, glittering powder found on exposed surfaces of the Hoshimori Plateau during the peak of Hikarishō, when the dragon auroras touch the ground. The powder is warm, faintly luminescent, and dissolves completely into food. The flavor is impossible to describe in conventional terms — those who have tasted it say it changes every time, and that the meal it seasons feels significant in a way ordinary food does not. Terrain: Hoshimori Plateau — during Hikarishō peak only Yield: 1 portion per successful forage Weight: — per portion | Cost: not sold

Inochi no Shio (Salt of Life) A crystalline substance found at the exact point where sei-active spring water meets volcanic mineral deposits — a convergence so specific that fewer than a dozen sites in all of Kagekuni produce it. The crystals form slowly and are self-replenishing, but harvesting too aggressively depletes the site for years. The flavor is warmth, vitality, and something that sits beyond the tongue's ability to categorize. Meals seasoned with it produce effects that border on the miraculous. Terrain: Specific sei-volcanic convergence sites (known locations: one in Hi, one in Sora, others rumored) Yield: 1 portion per successful forage Weight: — per portion | Cost: not sold

V. Staples & Preserved Goods — Shushoku (主食)

These are the carried, purchased, and cultivated foodstuffs that form the backbone of every traveller's pack. Unlike the foraged categories, staples are acquired through commerce, inheritance, or gift — not skill with a foraging kit. They are organised by rarity to reflect availability: common staples fill every market, while the rare and very rare represent treasures of craft, lineage, or ceremony that few travellers will ever taste.

Common

Kome (Rice) The foundation of nearly every meal in Kagekuni. White polished rice is carried by all travellers in small cloth bags and purchased in any settlement. Peasant households stretch it with brown rice or mixed grains; samurai eat it white. Quality varies subtly by province — Tsuchi rice is said to be the finest for daily eating, while Kusa's slightly sweeter grain is favoured for festival dishes. A traveller without kome in their pack is a traveller who expects hospitality. Availability: Universal — any settlement Source: Lowland rice paddies and terraced mountain fields Weight: 1 lb per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Miso Fermented soybean paste, sold by weight in wooden tubs or wrapped in bamboo leaves for travel. The foundation of soups, glazes, and braises, miso colour ranges from pale yellow (young, sweet) to deep red-brown (aged, assertive). It keeps indefinitely in a dry container and forgives all manner of cooking sins. A small pot of miso makes the difference between a sad camp meal and a proper one. Availability: Any settlement with a market Source: Fermented from soybeans, salt, and kōji mold Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Dried Dashi — Seaweed & Fish Stock Small bricks or loose powders of concentrated stock base, combining dried kombu kelp with katsuobushi flakes or occasionally dried sardines. A pinch dissolved in hot water produces instant broth — the backbone of every road meal from mushroom soup to trail ramen. Lightweight, compact, and keeps almost indefinitely. Availability: Coastal settlements, market towns, any roadside inn Source: Processed from dried kelp and smoked fish in coastal workshops Weight: — per portion | Cost: 3 cp

Sake Rice wine sold in small ceramic or bamboo flasks for travel. Drunk cold in summer and warm in winter, sake is also a cornerstone of cooking — a splash in broth, a rinse for fish, a glaze for grilled meat. Common grades are cheap and functional; named breweries command meaningful premiums. Every traveller carries at least a small flask, if only for the warming sip after a hard day's walk. Availability: Any settlement Source: Brewed from rice and kōji mold in breweries throughout Hokori Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 5 cp

Rice Vinegar A clear, mildly acidic vinegar brewed from rice. Essential for pickles, dressings, and the proper preparation of sushi rice. Milder than most vinegars — it sharpens without dominating — and carried in small ceramic flasks on the road. A few drops in a bowl of rice transforms it. Availability: Any market settlement Source: Fermented from rice and kōji in market-town workshops Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Tsukemono — Pickled Vegetables An assortment of root vegetables, daikon, gourd, and leafy greens pickled in salt, vinegar, miso, or rice bran mash. Every region has its own tradition — Hi's fiery pepper pickles differ utterly from Sora's delicate salt-pickled turnip. Tsukemono keeps well on the road and adds colour, crunch, and acidity to otherwise monotonous trail meals. Availability: Any market settlement; every household Source: Home-pickled or purchased from specialty shops Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 3 cp

Dried Tofu Firm blocks of soybean curd dried in the open air, or freeze-dried in the mountain winters of Sora. Reconstitutes in broth to a spongy, flavour-absorbing texture. Favoured by travelling monks and mountain pilgrims as a lightweight protein that carries no moral weight, and by lowland travellers for its sheer practicality. Availability: Market settlements, Buddhist-influenced villages Source: Pressed, drained, and dried soybean curd Weight: — per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Mirin Sweet rice wine used exclusively for cooking, never for drinking. Mirin produces the characteristic glossy glaze on grilled fish and braised meats, and adds a subtle sweetness that refined sugar cannot replicate. Sold in small corked flasks in every market town — a small splash is enough to transform a simple glaze into something worth remembering. Availability: Any market settlement Source: Brewed from sweet rice and kōji in traditional breweries Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 1 sp

Udon & Soba Dried wheat noodles (udon) and buckwheat noodles (soba), sold in paper-wrapped bundles. Keep for weeks, cook in minutes. Soba is the mountain food — buckwheat grows where wheat cannot — while udon is the lowland staple, favoured for its softness and the way it holds a rich broth. A traveller of any province recognises both and knows when to carry which. Availability: Any market settlement Source: Milled, rolled, and cut in noodle workshops Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Goma-abura — Sesame Oil Pressed sesame oil in small stoppered flasks, amber-golden and carrying a deep nutty aroma that fills a campsite the moment the stopper is drawn. Used for frying and as a finishing drizzle. The scent alone can elevate the humblest campfire meal from mere sustenance to proper cooking. Availability: Market settlements, agricultural provinces Source: Cold-pressed from roasted sesame seeds Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 3 cp

Umeboshi — Pickled Plum Small, intensely salty-sour plums pickled in salt and red shiso leaves, wrapped individually in leaf or stored in small jars. A single umeboshi sharpens a bowl of plain rice, and travellers swear the fruit wards off road sickness, fevers, and ill intentions. Keeps for years — many households preserve the same crock across generations. Availability: Any market settlement; every household Source: Preserved plums from lowland orchards, typically home-cured Weight: — per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Nori — Dried Laver Sheets of dried and lightly toasted laver seaweed, pressed flat and bundled in paper. Nori wraps rice balls, shreds over noodles, and lines sushi rolls. It keeps almost forever in a dry bundle and weighs next to nothing. Harvested along the Nami and Mizu coasts and traded inland along the Emperor's Highway to every market town. Availability: Coastal villages, market settlements Source: Farmed and wild-harvested from coastal rocks, dried on bamboo frames Weight: — per portion | Cost: 3 cp

Katsuobushi — Dried Bonito Flakes Smoked, dried, and shaved skipjack tuna, sold in paper packets of paper-thin flakes. Distinct from dried dashi blocks — katsuobushi is used as a finishing topping on hot food, where the flakes curl and "dance" in the rising steam as though the fish were alive again. A cornerstone of Mizu and Nami cooking and the defining flavour of ocean-touched cuisine. Availability: Coastal settlements, quality markets inland Source: Smoked and dried by specialised coastal workshops Weight: — per portion | Cost: 4 cp

Azuki — Red Beans Small, dark red beans sold by the handful or in larger cloth bags. Boiled into porridge for autumn mornings, sweetened for festival confections, or cooked with mochigome for ceremonial red rice. A peasant staple throughout the agricultural provinces — cheap, filling, and keeping indefinitely. The dark soup made from them carries ceremonial significance at certain seasonal observances. Availability: Any market settlement Source: Cultivated in the lowland fields of Tsuchi, Kusa, and Hana Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 1 cp

Mochigome — Sweet Rice A glutinous variant of rice used for mochi, festival dishes, and celebratory meals. Heavier and stickier than ordinary kome when cooked, with a distinctive chewiness that ordinary rice lacks. Commanded as ceremonial food in noble households and shrines. Sold in smaller bags at slightly higher prices than common rice, it marks the difference between a weekday meal and a celebration. Availability: Market settlements, shrine towns Source: Cultivated alongside ordinary rice in select paddies Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 3 cp

Komugi-ko — Wheat Flour Ground wheat from the lowland farms of Tsuchi and Hana, sold in paper-wrapped bricks or loose in cloth bags. Heavier and less refined than the whiter flours of urban kitchens, but entirely sufficient for noodles, dumpling wrappers, and the tempura batters of market stalls. The grain itself carries the faint sweetness of lowland sun. Availability: Market settlements, agricultural provinces Source: Stone-milled from wheat at rural grain mills Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 2 cp

Uncommon

Wasanbon — Refined Sugar Pale, extraordinarily fine sugar refined in small village cooperatives of southern Hana and Kusa, where the specific microclimate allows for the slow, patient crystallisation the product demands. Used sparingly in sweets, ceremonial confections, and the glaze of refined dishes. A luxury to most peasant households — a small paper packet of wasanbon is considered a generous gift to a host. Availability: Larger market towns, Heian, noble households Source: Hand-refined from sugarcane in small southern cooperatives Weight: — per portion | Cost: 2 sp

Junmai-shu — Pure-Rice Sake Premium sake brewed exclusively from rice, water, and kōji — no added distillate. Clean, bright, and deeply aromatic, with subtle variations between breweries. Named producers in Hana and Tsuchi mark their flasks with clan seals. Junmai-shu drinks well and cooks better, and a splash in a glaze can transform a competent dish into a memorable one. Merchants in Heian specifically stock it for noble clients. Availability: Upscale markets, named breweries, noble estates Source: Brewed in specific named breweries by traditional methods Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: 3 sp

Koikuchi-shōyu — Dark Soy Paste A deeper, more intense soy paste aged longer than common shōyu, with a darker colour and a more complex, almost smoky flavour profile. Used as a finishing sauce or in glazes where the depth of flavour matters more than the volume applied. Aged at least two years in wooden casks before being drawn off and bottled. A single drop on grilled fish shows the difference immediately. Availability: Quality markets, specialty vendors Source: Fermented and aged by traditional soy workshops Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 2 sp

Kōji — Rice Mold Starter A live fermentation culture — rice grains inoculated with the kōji mold that enables the production of sake, miso, shōyu, and countless other foods. Sold in small cloth-wrapped bundles by fermentation masters, who guard their specific strains carefully. A traveller with kōji, rice, and a few weeks can brew their own sake, miso, or pickles on the road — the beginning of a long and patient art. Availability: Specialty vendors, breweries, fermentation masters Source: Cultivated from mother strains in specialised workshops Weight: — per portion | Cost: 1 sp

Rare

Chōrei Miso — Longevity Miso A miso aged for over a century in cedar casks at specific Buddhist monasteries, passed from generation to generation of temple cooks who tend each cask as an inheritance. The colour is nearly black and the flavour is impossibly deep — a single spoonful transforms an entire pot of broth. The monks who tend the casks rarely sell chōrei miso for coin; it is more often given in exchange for service or as a gift to honoured guests. A small jar is a meaningful reward for a completed quest. Availability: Specific Buddhist monasteries; not openly sold Source: Aged for 100+ years in monastery cedar casks Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: 8 gp (informal) — traditionally given, not sold

Tennō-mai — Imperial Field Rice Rice grown exclusively at a single imperial holding outside Heian, tended by farming families whose lineage predates the current dynasty. Each grain is pearl-white and slightly larger than common rice, cooking into a texture that noble diners describe as "clouds made solid." A single gō (roughly six ounces) is a gift fit for a daimyo. Possession without authorisation is technically a punishable offence, though the law is rarely enforced against those who receive it as a gift. Availability: Imperial court, highest noble households, select Heian shops Source: Grown only at the Imperial Fields near Heian Weight: 1 lb per portion | Cost: 5 gp

Sanjūnen-shōyu — Thirty-Year Soy A soy sauce aged for three decades in a single cask, producing a liquid so concentrated that it is used drop by drop rather than poured. The flavour is almost savoury-sweet, with notes of dark caramel and deep earth. Only a handful of producers in Hana and Tsuchi have casks old enough to yield it, and each produces only a few small flasks per year. Purchased by Heian chefs at the start of each season. Availability: Specialty vendors in Heian, certain noble households Source: Aged thirty years in specific Hana and Tsuchi workshops Weight: — per portion | Cost: 6 gp

Hime-jio — Princess Salt A hand-crafted finishing salt produced in a single coastal village in Mizu, where an elderly matriarch and her apprentices evaporate seawater in shallow pans and sculpt each crystal by hand. Every grain is a perfect flake, with a subtle, almost floral brininess. Used as a finishing salt in the kitchens of noble households and the finest Heian restaurants. The matriarch reputedly turns away any buyer she deems unworthy of the craft. Availability: Specialty vendors; the village itself Source: Hand-crafted in a single Mizu coastal village Weight: — per portion | Cost: 4 gp

Very Rare

Ryū no Sake — Dragon's Sake Sake brewed in a single cask that was blessed at a Progenitor shrine generations ago and has been in continuous use ever since. The rice is Tennō-mai, the water is drawn from a sei-active spring, and the fermentation is tended by a master brewer who inherited the position from their grandmother. The finished sake is faintly luminescent in dim light, and those who drink it describe a sensation of warmth settling into the bones. Served only at imperial observances and the highest Shinto ceremonies — never sold, and given only as the most meaningful of gifts. Availability: Imperial court, high Shinto ceremonies; never sold Source: A single Progenitor-blessed cask at an ancient brewery Weight: ½ lb per portion | Cost: not sold

Kagami Mochi no Shinsei — Sacred Mirror Mochi Ceremonial mochi prepared once per year at specific Shinto shrines during the turning of the year. The rice is pounded by priests in ritual silence, and the finished mochi is placed upon the shrine altar for seven days before being divided among the shrine community. Those who receive a piece are said to be blessed by the ancestors for the year to come. Mortal travellers almost never obtain it; when they do, it is because a priest has chosen to honour them specifically. Availability: Specific Shinto shrines; distributed only at year's turning Source: Ritual preparation at ancestral shrines Weight: ¼ lb per portion | Cost: not sold

Hoshiyo-jio — Starlit Salt A salt evaporated under the Hoshimori aurora during the peak of Hikarishō, when the dragon auroras touch the ground. The process takes an entire season and can only be completed by the observatory communities of Sora, who time their pans to the celestial alignments with instruments older than any living seimaster. The finished crystals glow faintly in darkness and carry a flavour that shifts with the stars overhead. Used only in the most extraordinary meals — once in a lifetime, if at all. Availability: Hoshimori observatory; gifted, not sold Source: Evaporated seawater on the Hoshimori Plateau during Hikarishō Weight: — per portion | Cost: not sold

Ingredient Spoilage

Fresh ingredients spoil if not used within a reasonable time. Assume the foll

Type

Status
canonical

This document establishes the canonical timeline of the sei drought and Great Aphelion, the orbital mechanics of the Miyosai trinary system, and the orrery projection sequence as observed through the Hoshikagami no Ma. Content here supersedes or supplements existing entries in world.md, magic.md, and mechanical-arcane-orrery.md.

Canonical Timeline

Date Event
~12605 War of Fractured Banners begins; stellar decline starts as Susanoo and Tsukuyomi begin their long retreat
~12806 First secondary star lost to naked-eye visibility; dark ages begin
13088 Temple of Oryuzan Tenku-ji falls; surviving worshipers depart
~14344 Great Aphelion — all three stars at maximum mutual distance; absolute nadir of the dark ages
~15883 First secondary star returns to naked-eye visibility; dark ages end; dawn
~15962 First Talents emerge; sei accessible again in rare individuals
~16693 Great Awakening — all three stars clearly visible; sei fully restored
16744 Current campaign date — 51 years post-Awakening

The dark ages span ~12806 to ~15883 — approximately 3,077 years, with the Great Aphelion at their midpoint. The decline preceding them runs 201 years. The return arc from dawn to Great Awakening runs 810 years.

The Miyosai Trinary System — Orbital Mechanics

Structure

The Miyosai system is a gravitationally bound trinary stellar system. All three stars orbit a common barycenter — the true gravitational center of the system. Amaterasu is the most massive of the three and carries its planetary family with it as it completes its barycentric orbit. Seizan, as one of those planets, travels with Amaterasu.

Barycenter (common gravitational center)
├── Amaterasu — orbits barycenter on its own inclined plane
│   └── Planetary system — orbits Amaterasu (includes Seizan)
│       └── Moons — orbit Seizan
├── Susanoo — orbits barycenter on its own inclined plane
└── Tsukuyomi — orbits barycenter on its own inclined plane

The three stars travel on different orbital inclinations relative to each other, producing a three-dimensional dance rather than a flat orbital disc. Each star's position in Seizan's sky shifts continuously as all three complete their individual barycentric orbits. The named astrological events in the existing record — Nagorikaze, Long Shadow — are the routine expressions of this dance: individual stars reaching notable positions within normal orbital variation.

Planetary and Lunar Behavior

Because the planets orbit Amaterasu and travel with it, the seven planets do not participate in the Great Aphelion. Their positions relative to Seizan shift only in their normal orbital patterns around Amaterasu throughout the drought period. The moons, which orbit Seizan directly, are similarly unaffected by the positions of Susanoo and Tsukuyomi.

In the orrery, this means planetary and lunar armatures continue their normal motion through the entire dark ages period. The sei drought is visible in the orrery as exclusively a two-star withdrawal — Susanoo and Tsukuyomi receding while everything else continues its ordinary dance. This is more striking than a general dimming: the machine keeps working, the planets keep moving, and two of the three stars are simply not where they should be.

Why the Great Aphelion Is Singular

Under normal orbital conditions, the three stars periodically reach individual far points from each other — this is routine. The Great Aphelion requires three independent conditions to align simultaneously:

  • Amaterasu at maximum distance from the barycenter on one side of its orbit, carrying Seizan with it
  • Susanoo at maximum distance on the opposing side of its orbital arc
  • Tsukuyomi at maximum distance on the opposing extreme of its own inclined arc

Because the three orbital periods and inclinations are entirely independent, the probability of all three peaking simultaneously is the product of three separate low-probability alignments. More critically, the compounding is geometric rather than additive — when Amaterasu swings to its extreme, it carries Seizan away from the barycenter; Susanoo and Tsukuyomi simultaneously reaching their opposing extremes means Seizan is not simply far from two stars, but has been actively carried in the opposite direction while they retreated. The distance at nadir is the sum of three orbital extremes working against each other.

This event has been recorded once — imperfectly, in fragmentary form. The possibility of a future occurrence exists but is considered by any scholar who has assembled the relevant data to be a matter for timescales beyond meaningful planning.

Individual Star Orbital Profiles

Amaterasu — The Anchor

Mass: Primary; largest of the three stars. Orbit: Moves around the barycenter, but its greater mass means the barycenter sits relatively close to it — Amaterasu's orbital movement is the least dramatic of the three. Its planetary family travels with it throughout. Sei signature: Core life energy; baseline sei. Foundational and stable. Projection color: Golden-yellow. During the drought: Never goes dark. Amaterasu's projection in the orrery holds throughout the entire drought period. It is the one point of gold that remains in the dome regardless of what date the operator sets. This is why the dark ages were cultural and intellectual collapse rather than extinction — Amaterasu's baseline sei sustained life, agriculture, and the physical world while the more complex magical expressions that depended on the full trinary system became inaccessible.

Tsukuyomi — First to Fade, Last to Return

Mass: Larger deep-red dwarf; second most massive. Orbit: Elongated barycentric orbit — already has the most dramatic near-far swing of the three under normal conditions. Long Shadow events are the routine expression of this elongation. During the Great Aphelion, the elongation compounds to an extreme that no living record had prepared the order to anticipate. Sei signature: Transformation magic, energy manipulation. Projection color: Deep red.

Fade sequence: Tsukuyomi's deep red begins bleeding from the orrery's projection approximately 150–170 years before the Great Aphelion nadir (~14174–14194). Because its elongated orbit already produces dramatic near-far variation, the early stages of its decline would have been logged by the order as an unusually extended Long Shadow before the true nature of the event became clear. Practitioners of the period would have noticed transformation magic becoming unreliable first — the most complex sei expressions failing before the simpler ones.

Return sequence: Because its orbit is the most elongated, Tsukuyomi's return is the slowest. Its deep red is the last color to reappear in the orrery during the recovery arc — faint and intermittent for centuries before becoming reliable. The moment all three stars are clearly visible simultaneously, which defines the Great Awakening (~16693), is effectively the moment Tsukuyomi's red crosses the threshold of clarity. It is the completion of the return, not its beginning.

Susanoo — Second to Fade, First to Return

Mass: Smallest blue-white dwarf. Orbit: Complex barycentric orbit — not elongated like Tsukuyomi's, but highly variable. Produces both the closest approaches (Nagorikaze) and meaningful retreats. Being the least massive of the three, its sei output is the most sensitive to distance. Sei signature: Water magic, healing, purification. Projection color: Blue-white.

Fade sequence: Susanoo's blue-white dims approximately 50–80 years before the Great Aphelion nadir (~14264–14294). The order would have watched Tsukuyomi declining for nearly a century before Susanoo began to follow. Susanoo's failure was the loss that reached the general population — healers losing effectiveness, coastal and maritime practices becoming unreliable. Tsukuyomi's decline was a practitioner problem; Susanoo's was a human one.

Return sequence: Because its orbit is complex rather than elongated, Susanoo's return path is more direct. It is the first secondary star to show meaningful recovery in the orrery — a faint but perceptible blue-white appearing in the dome while Tsukuyomi's arm remains dark. Susanoo's return is the first confirmation that the system is correcting rather than continuing to deteriorate. The first Talents (15962) emerge after dawn (15883) and correlate with Susanoo's partial return, consistent with healing and purification being among the earliest accessible sei expressions.

Orrery Projection Sequence

What the party observes when scrolling through the dial. Mechanical armature motion continues normally throughout — only the arcane projection layer responds to sei availability.

Pre-Decline (pre-~12605)

All three stars project at full intensity. Amaterasu golden-yellow at center. Susanoo's blue-white and Tsukuyomi's deep red visible on their respective inclined armature planes. Planets and moons in full normal motion around Amaterasu's family. The dome is warm and fully lit — this is the room functioning as it was designed to function. When the party scrolls to a Golden Age date, they understand for the first time what they have been looking at in its damaged state.

Early Decline (~12605–12700)

Tsukuyomi's deep red begins to bleed at the edges. Subtle — a skilled operator would notice the color temperature shifting before they could name it. A pre-existing Long Shadow event during this period would have been logged by the order as unusually extended before the deeper pattern was recognized. Susanoo holds full brightness. The dome is visibly but not dramatically wrong.

Deepening Decline (~12700–12806)

Tsukuyomi's red is clearly diminished — no longer a question of interpretation. The dome feels unbalanced in a way that is difficult to articulate. Susanoo still holds, which means the order would have had reason to hope the event was limited to Tsukuyomi's orbit. The first star crosses below naked-eye visibility threshold at approximately 12806. Dark ages begin.

Late Decline / Early Dark Ages (~12806–14264)

Tsukuyomi's arm is dark. Susanoo still holds its blue-white in the orrery projection, though dimming as it approaches its own far point. The dome is now Amaterasu's gold, Susanoo's fading blue-white, and one silent arm. The operator's log from this period — if it survived — would be increasingly terse.

Susanoo's Failure / Approach to Nadir (~14264–14344)

Susanoo's projection dims and goes dark. The dome is now Amaterasu alone. All planetary and lunar armatures continue their ordinary motion — the machine still works — but the two secondary stars are bare bronze. The room does not feel like an observatory. It feels like something else.

Great Aphelion (~14344)

All three stars at maximum mutual distance. Amaterasu's armature sits at one extreme of its barycentric arc, the planetary family clustered around it. Susanoo's armature sits at the opposing extreme on its inclined plane. Tsukuyomi's armature sits at its own opposing extreme on its differently inclined plane. Three separate arms on three separate planes, all pointing away from each other. The geometry of the event is legible in the mechanism before the party processes the darkness — they can see why it was catastrophic. Amaterasu alone in the dome. The nadir.

Post-Nadir / Continuing Dark Ages (~14344–15883)

Scrolling forward through these years changes nothing visible. Amaterasu holds. The two secondary arms remain dark. Advancing decades — centuries — in seconds and seeing no change in the darkness has its own effect at the table. The absence is not passive.

Dawn (~15883)

Susanoo's armature shows the first ghost of blue-white. Not full projection — a faint shimmer, barely distinguishable from reflected light. A character with sei sensitivity (Relc, Ko'jiri, Sun Wukong) may feel warmth in their sternum before the light is visible to anyone. This is the moment the dark ages end — not because magic returns, but because the sky does. Sei remains largely inaccessible; the stars are simply back.

First Talents / Early Return (~15883–15962)

Susanoo's blue-white strengthens slowly. Tsukuyomi's arm remains dark. The dome is Amaterasu and a faint secondary light — the room no longer feels like the nadir, but it does not feel restored. When the party scrolls to ~15962, the first Talents date, they can see that sei's earliest return correlates with Susanoo having only partially recovered. The match between star position and magical accessibility is legible if they think to look for it.

Return Arc (~15962–16693)

Susanoo continues strengthening. Tsukuyomi's deep red begins its slower return — faint and intermittent for a long period before becoming reliable. Scrolling through this arc in the orrery, the party watches the dome gradually fill. The return does not feel like restoration — it feels like recovery from a very long illness.

Great Awakening (~16693)

Tsukuyomi's red crosses into clear, reliable visibility. All three stars present. This is the recognizable moment — a party member who has seen the Golden Age dates and then scrolled forward through centuries of darkness will feel the completion of this arc when all three lights are in the dome together again.

Current Date (16744)

The orrery shows the present sky. All three stars lit. Planetary and lunar armatures in their current positions. A party member who thinks to compare this against a deep Golden Age date may notice that Tsukuyomi's projection, while present, carries slightly less intensity than its pre-decline readings. The return is real. It is not yet complete. The orbital correction is still ongoing.

This is the only moment in the orrery sequence where the party is looking at their own world in real time. The comparison between then and now is available to them if they seek it.

text.content:
Master Timeline

Period Years Name
Pre-Imperial Before 8000 Age of Dragons
Imperial Founding ~8000–8611 Era of the First Emperors
First Golden Age 8611–13050 Kagekuni's Golden Age
Age of Strife 13050–13088 War of Fractured Banners
Dark Ages 13088–15642 The Long Dark
Recovery 15642–15691 Jinshō Reformation
Second Golden Age 15691–15757 Era of New Discovery
Subtle Awakening 15757–16620 Return of Talents
Great Awakening 16620–present Magic Restored
Current 16744 Post-Imperial Crisis

Key Historical Events

Age of Dragons (Pre-8000)

  • Seven dragon clans ruled the archipelago before human settlement
  • Early settlers integrated, paid tribute, joined clans
  • Intermingling produced near-immortal arcadian (elf) leaders — first daimyo
  • Dragons gradually withdrew from direct rule

Era of the First Emperors (~8000–8611)

  • Tenryū no Mikado ascended ~8000 at age 852; descended from Crimson and Golden Dragon bloodlines
  • United fragmented clans through diplomacy and martial campaigns
  • Key conflict: Crimson Clan (Akaryū) refused submission; withdrew into Akaho Sanmyaku; eastern faction joined empire; western lands became barbarian territory
  • Battle of Seirei Mizuumi — secured Kawa; defeated Azure Clan navy
  • Onyx Rebellion (8238–8611) — Kokuryū led 400-year guerrilla war from Tatara; ended with destruction of Kuroi Yama; Kokuryū escaped
  • Tenryū died 8694; succeeded by son Ryūhiko no Mikado (already 794 years old)

Golden Age (8611–13050)

  • Eight emperors; unprecedented peace and prosperity
  • Major constructions: Imperial Palace (Heian), Great Library (Seirei Mizuumi), Grand Canal (Mizushima), Hoshino Tō observatory (Shirogane Yama), Kokuyō Ryūkyūjō fortress (Tatara)
  • Emperor's Highway built 11248
  • Emperors: Tenryū, Ryūhiko, Seiryū, Byakuryū, Kinryū, Shoryū, Inaryū, Kōryū

War of Fractured Banners (13050–13088)

  • Tensions between Zirak and Glimfyr on Tatara spread empire-wide
  • Emperor Kōryū no Mikado slain on battlefield 13053
  • Son Ryūjin no Mikado II established the Shogunate; appointed first Shogun Kazutaka no Kazuhiko
  • Key battles: Defense of Midoriko, Pursuit to Kumoji, Campaign in Tatara, Burning of Shirotsuru, Siege of Fushichō, Ambush at Tatsumaki Gorge, Battle of the Thunder Plains
  • War ended 13062; Seiryu and Hagane clans wiped out; magic vanished completely

Dark Ages (13088–15642)

  • Rampant famine, disease, population decimation
  • Magic completely absent
  • Little documentation survives

Jinshō Reformation (15642–15691)

  • Emperor Jinshin no Mikado enacted sweeping reforms
  • Agricultural revival, infrastructure rebuilding, trade stimulation, educational revival
  • Great Library partially restored (had been destroyed by earthquake)
  • Established Kokushi Kyōkai with Seimu Daijin and Zaiumu Daijin

Era of New Discovery (15691–15757)

  • Expedition of 15691 led by Admiral Taira no Akinori and General Tokugawa no Ryuji
  • Diplomat Hōjō no Kaoru also key figure; later became first Gaikō Daijin
  • Discovered lands beyond Kagekuni; returned with slaves, precious metals, new knowledge
  • 150+ expeditions over next 60 years; clan rivalries intensified
  • Emperor appointed Minamoto no Katsuro (Tenshiko Clan) as Shogun ~16012
  • Shogun enacted: Expedition Regulation Act, Resource Distribution Act, Peace and Mediation Act, Defense Enhancement Act
  • Shogunate retired; Gaikō Daijin established under Hōjō no Kaoru

Era of Subtle Awakening (15757–16620)

  • Talents (individuals with innate magic) began emerging ~15757
  • First known Talent: Hikari no Kenta — storm magic; born 15757
  • Talents persecuted; formed underground communities
  • Notable Talents: Mizuki no Hana (Gekkō Clan; shadow magic), Fujimoto no Aiko (Ryūkaze Clan; wind manipulation)
  • Seishin Enclave founded on Unmeijima; grew into city of Seishin
  • Hikari no Shizuku — healing/light magic enclave within Heian
  • Epoch of Factional Flux (16204–16434): Clans merged, dissolved, restructured
    • Hōjō Clan civil war → merger with Minamoto → became Clan Kaminari (honoring Raijin)
    • Ryūkaze Clan absorbed smaller clans; dominant in northwest
    • Yamamoto Clan splintered; Ishikawa Clan dissolved
    • Clan Tetsujin emerged as mercenary clan from Ishikawa remnants
  • Peasant Uprising (16442–16461): Sparked by crackdown at Midoriko village
    • Shogun Takeda no Hiroshi appointed 16443
    • First Fukushi Daijin: Hayashi no Haruto appointed 16453
    • Combined military/diplomatic approach ended uprising 16461
  • Plague Campaign of Kuroyami (16609–16616):
    • Kuroyami no Akuma (formerly Takeda no Arata) found necromantic tome in Kuroshi Temple, Yurei
    • Established Eikyū Yami Clan cult; led undead legions
    • Shogun Minamoto no Katsuro appointed 16610; recruited Talents
    • Seishin Enclave, Raimeiin, Forest of Spirits publicly revealed themselves
    • Kuroyami defeated but never captured — escaped; whereabouts unknown
    • Eikyū Yami Clan persists in some form

Great Awakening (16620–present)

  • Magic officially returned ~16687 — daimyo actively recruit mages

• Reforms of Ryūjin no Mikado (16732): 18th emperor; last near-immortal elf; banned Kokushi Kyōkai from appointing Shogun without imperial approval
  • End of Imperial Line (16739): Ryūjin no Mikado died under mysterious circumstances; officially old age; foul play suspected but unproven
  • Widespread Aggression (16742): War between Genso and Arashi alliances begins
  • Current Year: 16744
