text.content:
Sei Fundamentals

  • Sei = magic energy flowing through all living things
  • Present throughout Seizan; expressed through celestial alignment and natural forces
  • Began declining during the War of Fractured Banners era (~12605); first secondary star lost to visibility ~12806; effectively inaccessible by ~13088 (when the last major sei institution — Oryuzan Tenku-ji — fell)
  • Period without accessible sei lasted approximately 3,077 years (12806–15883)
  • Slowly returned through Talents from ~15962
  • Fully restored ~16693 (Great Awakening)
  • The drought's cause is officially unknown; scholars debate whether it was consequence of the war itself or a natural cycle

Seimasters

  • Arcane scholars and researchers — not necessarily practitioners
  • Study sei as discipline; map, theorize, document celestial alignments
  • Title connotes scholarship over power
  • A non-casting seimaster may outrank a gifted practitioner socially
  • Some manifest as wizards, sorcerers, monks in D&D terms
  • Study in mountaintop monasteries

Magical Factions (Publicly Known)

  • Seishin (City, Unmeijima) — premier magical research institution
  • Raimeiin (雷鳴院 — Institute of Thunder) — publicly declared during Plague Campaign
  • Forest of Spirits — publicly declared during Plague Campaign
  • Hikari no Shizuku — healing/light magic; operates within Heian

Kuroyami no Akuma

  • Formerly Takeda no Arata
  • Found necromantic tome in Kuroshi Temple, Yurei
  • Led Plague Campaign 16609–16616
  • Defeated but never captured or killed — escaped; whereabouts unknown
  • Eikyū Yami Clan persists

The Sei Drought and the Great Aphelion

The sei drought was not caused by the War of Fractured Banners — it coincided with the Great Aphelion, a once-in-millennia event in which all three stars of the Miyosai trinary system reached maximum mutual distance from their common barycenter simultaneously. The planets, which orbit Amaterasu and travel with it, did not participate — nor did the moons, which orbit Seizan directly. The event was exclusively a three-star separation across three independent orbital inclinations, compounding geometrically.

The true timeline: stellar decline began 12605; dark ages started ~12806 (first star lost to visibility); the temple fell in 13088; the Great Aphelion nadir occurred ~14344; dawn (first star returned) ~15883; First Talents ~15962; Great Awakening ~16693. The drought spanned approximately 3,077 years (12806–~15883).

The causal chain (aphelion → slumber → drought, or aphelion → both) is unknown even to the Ancient Guard. The slow orbital return of the secondary stars correlates with sei's gradual restoration — but the orbital correction is not yet complete.

See also: core/world.md [SEALED] — The Great Aphelion and the Sei Drought; core/great-aphelion.md — full canonical timeline and orbital mechanics.

Murasakiryū's Sei Awareness

Every sei use in Kagekuni passes through the awakened Progenitor Murasakiryū's awareness. This means every spell the party casts, every druidic invocation, every monk ability — all of it is potentially observed. The implications for Ko'jiri's sorcery, Relc's druidic power, and Sun Wukong's ki are significant but unexplored.

Key question (unresolved): Does Murasakiryū actively monitor individual sei users, or is it passive background awareness? Does the party register as notable?

text.content:
Type
system-reference

In Kagekuni, nothing is taken lightly from the land. A hunter who kills a deer owes the forest an accounting. A smith who pulls iron from the mountain asks the stone's permission before the first strike of the pick. A cook who gathers mountain sage bows to the plant before cutting. The materials of the world are not commodities — they are borrowed, and the borrower is expected to honor the source.

This document is the canonical reference for every material that can be gathered, harvested, mined, scavenged, or otherwise pulled from the world of Kagekuni, and for the mechanics that govern both their gathering and their use in craft. It is the DM's single source of truth. When Foundry item definitions are generated, they are generated from this file. When a recipe in core/recipes.md references an ingredient, it references a Part I entry here. When a player asks "what can I forage in the cedar forest," the answer comes from Part II.

How This Document Works

The file is organized in two parts.

Part I — The Material Catalogue. Every material has a single authoritative entry, organized by category. Part I is the source of truth for what a material is: its name, rarity, weight, value, grade variants, preservation rules, descriptions, and DM notes. Part I never describes where a material comes from — that belongs in Part II.

Part II — Gathering & Yield Tables. The mechanic for harvesting materials, the five activities used to gather them, the grade system at the point of harvest, failure modes for both gathering and crafting, the seasons and seasonal events of Kagekuni, the biomes of the archipelago and what each one yields, and the named beast harvests that produce one-time legendary rewards.

Cross-references between the two halves use markdown anchors: [Ōkami-niku](#ōkami-niku). Part II tables link back to Part I entries so the DM can jump from "what did they find" to "what does that mean" in one click.

Knowledge Tiers

All Part I entries respect the campaign's three-tier knowledge system:

  • [KNOWN] — Information the players have learned through play. Safe to reference anywhere.
  • [DISCOVERABLE] — Exists in-world and could be learned. Lives in the DM Notes section of each entry. Quest seeds marked
QUEST SEED . - [SEALED] — Campaign-level secrets. Never surface in player-facing descriptions. Mark undecided elements as TBD.

The player-facing description field of each entry is always safe to export to Foundry or share with players. The DM Notes field is never exported.

On Grades and Foundry

Every material that supports grading exists as four distinct Foundry items — one per grade (並 Nami, 上 Jō, 特上 Tokujō, 極上 Gokujō). Within this document, a material has a single Part I entry with a Grade Variants sub-block listing the four tiers, their value multipliers, their craft modifiers, and reserved Foundry item ID slots. The 4× proliferation exists only in Foundry. This file remains the single source of truth. The full grade system is documented in Part II.

Part I — The Material Catalogue

Part I is divided into twelve categories. Some will start full; others (Sen'i, Hōseki, Ekitai) will begin mostly empty and fill as the campaign surfaces new materials. Every entry follows the schema documented at the end of this Part I header.

Part I Entry Schema (Reference)

Every Part I entry must use this schema. Fields in square brackets are optional and may be omitted if irrelevant.

### [Material Name] ([日本語名]) ([English Gloss])

**Category:** Niku | Yakusō | Kinoko | Chōmiryō | Shushoku | Kegawa | Hone | Sen'i | Kōseki | Hōseki | Mokuzai | Ekitai
**Rarity:** Common (並) | Uncommon (上) | Rare (特上) | Very Rare (極上) | Legendary (伝説) | Artifact (神器)
**Source Type:** Foraged | Hunted | Mined | Harvested | Scavenged | One-Time | Purchased
**Biomes:** [list of biomes where found, referencing Part II biome names]
**Seasons:** Haru | Natsu | Aki | Fuyu | All | [or seasonal event tag like Hikarishō]
**Yield per Success:** [e.g., "1d4 per resource point" or "fixed: 1 sample"]
**Weight:** [per portion/unit]
**Base Value:** [gold pieces per unit, before grade multiplier]
**Preservation:** [fresh shelf life / preserved shelf life]
**Tool Proficiency:** [tool needed to harvest or process, if any]
[**Restrictions:** any legal, cultural, or ritual constraints on harvest]

#### Grade Variants

| Grade | Value Multiplier | Craft Modifier | Foundry Item ID |
|---|---|---|---|
| 並 Nami (Run-of-the-mill) | ×0.75 | −2 | tbd |
| 上 Jō (Clean / Standard) | ×1.0 | +0 | tbd |
| 特上 Tokujō (High-Purity) | ×1.5 | +2 | tbd |
| 極上 Gokujō (Legendary Bloom) | ×2.5 | +5 or advantage on craft check | tbd |

*Legendary and Artifact materials may specify a fixed grade; see individual entries.*

#### Description (Player-Facing)

Sensory, evocative, spoiler-free prose. This is what a player with full knowledge sees in Foundry when they inspect the item. Never contains [DISCOVERABLE] or [SEALED] content.

#### Unidentified Description

What the item looks like to a player who has *not* identified it — found in a crate, pulled from a beast with no naming knowledge, sitting on a shrine altar. Visual and tactile description only. Foundry shows this to players who have not yet identified the material.

#### Image Prompt

Prompt for watercolor-style token generation. Should evoke the material without depicting a specific shape or branded pose. Muted natural palette. Soft edges. The image is a suggestion of the thing, not a catalog photograph.

#### Used In

*(This section is auto-populated by the reindex skill by crawling recipes.md. Do not edit manually.)*

#### DM Notes

Lore, ecology, cultural significance, harvesting taboos, plot hooks, alternate uses. May contain **[KNOWN]**, **[DISCOVERABLE]**, or **[SEALED]** content with tier markers. This field is never exported to Foundry player-facing descriptions.

Structural note. Category headers are ##, rarity tier headers within categories use bold text (not ###), individual material entries use ###, and entry subsections use ####. This keeps the markdown outline navigable and avoids collision between category and entry header levels.

Niku 肉 — Meat & Edible Animal Products

The meat of Kagekuni runs the full span from humble river fish to the heart of a mountain god. Hunting traditions are deeply tied to the warrior caste — the samurai on a hunt is not pursuing food but practicing the discipline of the kill — while fishing and small-game trapping belong to the peasantry and to the half-feral communities of the deep forest. Edible organs carry their own significance; the liver of a bear is a gift to an elder, the heart of a killed enemy is a ritual offering, and certain rare beasts yield parts that are considered medicine more than food.

Common

Yama-usagi 山兎 (Mountain Hare)

Category: Niku Rarity: Common (並) Source Type: Hunted Biomes: Satoyama, Sugi no Mori, Fumoto Seasons: All Yield per Success: 1d4 per resource point Weight: 1 lb per portion Base Value: 1 sp per portion Preservation: 2 days fresh; 14 days smoked or salted Tool Proficiency: Simple weapons or snares; cook's utensils for butchering

Lean, dark-rose meat from the wild hares that populate Hokori's lower forests and upland meadows. The flavour is clean and faintly grassy — not gamey, not strong, but distinctly wild. A single hare feeds two travellers well with rice.

A field-dressed small mammal, perhaps four to six pounds, pale rose flesh with darker muscle striping along the haunches. The smell is faint — clean meat, a trace of woodland soil.

Common throughout Hokori's forested provinces. Hunters set snares along known game trails in lower Fumoto and within any Satoyama. A Wisdom (Survival) check with trapper's tools yields the best results; bow hunting works at higher cost in time.

Small freshwater crabs pulled from clear streams and the edges of rice paddies. The shells are dark mottled green in life, turning vivid orange when cooked. Sweet, briny flesh inside a shell that must be cracked with fingers or the butt of a knife. Grilled whole, their flavour intensifies into something far greater than their size suggests.

Small armored arthropods, palm-sized, with dark mottled shells and pincers held defensively. They clack faintly when disturbed.

Gathered by hand from clear streams and paddy margins. Peasant children often harvest them as a side activity during other work. Fishing tackle not required. Best yields immediately after rainfall.

Small ground-dwelling birds hunted in grasslands, scrub, and the margins of cultivated fields. The meat is darker than chicken and carries a slightly mineral sweetness — perfect for a single-skewer meal over a cooking fire.

Small plucked game birds, each no larger than a fist, with pale-to-rose flesh and tiny bones. Faint scent of grass and warm feathers.

Slender river fish prized for the distinctive cucumber-melon scent of their flesh in the height of summer. Grilled whole on a split-bamboo skewer over charcoal, salted simply, the belly fat melts and the skin crisps. The single most perfect expression of a summer river in Hokori.

Slim silver-green fish, eight to ten inches long, with delicate iridescent scales and the faint melon scent that rises from them as they warm.

Watercolor of several small silver river fish laid on a bamboo mat, damp and glistening. Pale blue-green palette with hints of copper along the flanks. Gentle ripples suggested in wash behind them.

The quintessential summer river fish. Tradition holds the very best ayu come from the upper Kinryūgawa in late Natsu. A master fisher can catch them bare-handed in shallow riffles; most use tackle or traditional cormorant fishing.

Small songbirds netted in cultivated fields and eaves of village houses. The meat is dark and intensely flavoured for its size, traditionally grilled whole on a skewer — head, bones, and all. A peasant's protein, eaten without ceremony.

Dark, palm-sized freshwater snails harvested from rice paddies and slow-moving streams. The meat is earthy, chewy, and carries a bitter-green finish that miso and sake soften into something worth eating. A staple of peasant cuisine in the rice provinces.

The copper-barred pheasants of Hokori's forested hills. Larger and richer than quail, with a deep-red breast meat that benefits from slow cooking or the sharp bright heat of the grill. A proud bird, hunted by lords as often as peasants.

Venison from Hokori's forest deer, dark and dense. The shoulder and haunch cuts slow-braise into tenderness; the tenderloin sears quickly and carries a clean iron flavour. Standard game meat throughout the wooded provinces, and the most reliable large-game harvest in the system.

Stout silver-bronze fish that fill every pond, paddy, and sluggish river in lowland Hokori. The flesh is mild and earthy and stands up to strong seasoning — miso, soy, and ginger are the traditional rescues. Peasant food elevated by time-honoured preparation.

Small silver ocean fish that run in vast schools along Hokori's coasts. The flesh is oily and strong-flavoured — hated by some, beloved by others. Grilled on a metal plate over coals until the skin crisps and the bones soften, they are the humble backbone of coastal Mizu and Nami kitchens.

Yakusō 薬草 — Herbs & Medicinal Plants

Yakusō covers culinary herbs, medicinal plants, teas, and any green gathered for its flavor, scent, or healing property. The boundary with Kinoko is soft — many traditional formulas combine the two — and the boundary with Chōmiryō is cultural rather than botanical. A mountain sage is Yakusō; a sage dried, ground, and mixed into a spice blend is Chōmiryō. The distinction is use, not species. Herbal knowledge in Kagekuni is concentrated in the shrine maiden tradition and in the scattered communities of forest-dwelling druids, with village healers working from whatever lineage their teacher left them.

Kinoko 茸 — Mushrooms & Fungi

The fungi of Kagekuni's forests are prized beyond their weight in silver. Some are food, some are medicine, some are sei-resonant and used in the preparations of seimasters, and a few are lethally poisonous in ways that imitate the safe ones precisely enough to kill the careless. Mushroom gathering is a trained art; a forager who cannot distinguish the ryūkinoko from its deadly mimic does not forage for long. The best flushes follow the tsuyu-no-toki rains of early summer, and the deep cedar forests of Kaze produce varieties that grow nowhere else.

Chōmiryō 調味料 — Seasonings & Fermented Goods

Salt, miso, soy sauce, vinegar, rice wine for cooking, dried spice blends, fermented pastes, pickled vegetables. The backbone of every Kagekuni kitchen and the element that most distinguishes regional cooking. A Mizu fisherman's stew and a Tsuchi farmer's stew may share every other ingredient and still taste nothing alike because of the Chōmiryō applied. Fermentation is considered a sacred art — the kōji mold that underpins miso, soy sauce, sake, and a dozen other staples is sometimes described as a gift of the kami, and an old fermentation house is tended like a shrine.

Shushoku 主食 — Staples, Grains & Cooking Fats

Rice in all its varieties, wheat and barley in the north and south, millet in the poor mountain soil, and the rendered fats that every kitchen relies on. Oils from pressed seeds, lard from butchered pigs, rendered beast-fats from large game, and clarified butter from the few herds that exist on Hokori's high pastures. Shushoku is the foundation of every meal — everything else is applied to the staple, not the other way around. Rice especially carries weight far beyond its nutrition: a bowl of rice is a political act, the grain is an object of veneration in shrine offerings, and the control of rice paddies is the single most important lever of power in rural Kagekuni.

Kegawa 毛皮 — Hides, Pelts & Leather

Kegawa is primarily a secondary-harvest category: almost every Niku entry with a mammalian source yields hide material as part of the butchering process. Hone 骨 — Bone, Horn, Shell & Sinew

Like Kegawa, Hone is primarily a secondary-harvest category — nearly every hunted animal yields bone material, and routine bones (deer antler, boar tusk, fish bone) will be catalogued as the campaign surfaces specific needs. Part II — Gathering & Yield Tables

Part II defines how materials are found and where. It is the mechanical heart of the gathering system and the reference the DM consults during play when a player declares they want to forage, hunt, mine, cut timber, or scavenge.

The Gathering Mechanic

Gathering in Kagekuni resolves in three stages. A full attempt takes one in-world hour and resolves with a single opportunity roll plus one to five yield rolls.

Stage 1 — Declare the Activity

Before any dice are rolled, the gathering character declares which of the five activities they are attempting. Each activity uses different skills, tools, and yield tables. A character pursues only one activity per attempt — an hour spent foraging herbs does not incidentally yield game, ore, or timber. A character who wants to gather across categories must spend multiple attempts.

The five activities are:

  • Saishū 採集 — Foraging. Hunting for plants, fungi, fruits, nuts, and small surface materials. Skill: Wisdom (Survival) or Intelligence (Nature). Tool: Herbalism kit recommended; a failure without proficiency imposes disadvantage on the opportunity roll. Yields from: Yakusō, Kinoko, some Shushoku, some Ekitai, occasional Sen'i.
  • Shuryō 狩猟 — Hunting. Pursuing game of any size, on land or in water. Both land hunting and fishing fall under Shuryō — a rabbit snare and a river line are mechanically the same activity for the purposes of the gathering system. Skill: Wisdom (Survival). Tool: weapons or fishing tackle. Yields from: Niku, Kegawa, Hone, occasional Ekitai.
  • Saikutsu 採掘 — Mining. Extracting ore, stone, and gems from surface deposits, cave walls, riverbed gravel, or spoil heaps. Skill: Strength (Athletics) or Intelligence (Investigation). Tool: miner's tools (mattock, pick, chisel). Yields from: Kōseki, Hōseki, sometimes Ekitai (thermal waters).
  • Batsuboku 伐木 — Timber Harvest. Cutting wood, stripping bark, collecting sap and resin. Skill: Wisdom (Survival) or Strength (Athletics). Tool: woodcarver's or carpenter's tools. Yields from: Mokuzai, some Sen'i (plant fibers), some Ekitai (saps, resins).
  • Kaishū 回収 — Scavenging. Searching ruins, battlefields, abandoned sites, crashed carts, refuse heaps, and the fringes of civilization for useful materials of any category. Skill: Intelligence (Investigation). Tool: none required. Yields from: any category, depending on the site — a ruined temple yields different things from a battlefield, a burned farmhouse, or a shipwreck.

Stage 2 — The Opportunity Roll

Once the activity is declared, the character makes a single d20 check against the biome's Opportunity DC. This roll determines how productive the attempt was — not what was found.

Biome Tier Opportunity DC Example Biomes
Accessible 10 Satoyama, Tambo, lowland Kawa to Numa
Wild 13 Kaigan, Sugi no Mori, Fumoto, lower Murasaki-hara
Hostile 16 Takane, Kazan lower slopes, deep Murasaki-hara, Kōri-no-Mori
Otherworldly 20 Hoshimori Kōgen, Yōrin, Kazan summit, Seidorin, Haikyo (for sei-touched ruins)

The margin of success determines resource points — a pool of yield rolls the character gets to make.

Roll Result Resource Points Additional Effects
Fail (any margin) 0 Time lost. Roll on the failure-mode table for the biome tier.
Meet DC (0–4) 1 A productive session.
DC + 5 to 9 2 A good find.
DC + 10 to 14 3 An excellent find.
DC + 15 or more 4 An exceptional find.
Natural 20 (with bonus d10 per house rule) +1 bonus point Unlocks the Very Rare column of the yield table.
Total of 40+ — Unlocks Legendary yields where the table supports them. Most biome tables do not carry Legendary tiers; Legendary materials are usually tied to named-beast harvests in the dedicated section below.

Attempts per rest cycle. A character may make one gathering attempt per short rest and a maximum of two per long rest. If the party is traveling the same day, the maximum drops to one per long rest. Each attempt takes one in-world hour of focused effort.

Multiple activities per day. A character may pursue a different activity on a second attempt — morning hunt, afternoon forage — and each is rolled separately. An exceptional morning does not carry over into the afternoon. A character may not pursue the same activity twice in the same day in the same biome (the area is already worked); a second attempt must either be a different activity or a different biome.

Party gathering. Multiple characters may gather simultaneously, each rolling their own opportunity roll. Characters may use the Help action to grant advantage to a companion's opportunity roll in place of their own attempt, which is often the right play when one character is significantly more skilled than the others.

Stage 3 — The Yield Roll

For each resource point, the character rolls a d20 on the relevant biome-activity-season table in the Biomes of Kagekuni section below. Results are organized by rarity column:

  • 1–10 → Common
  • 11–17 → Uncommon
  • 18–19 → Rare
  • 20 → Very Rare (only if the Very Rare column is unlocked by the opportunity roll; otherwise re-roll as Rare)

If the biome, activity, or season combination is not supported, the attempt returns nothing — Saikutsu in an open wetland, Batsuboku on a volcanic glass field. Each biome entry lists which activities are supported and in which seasons.

Yield entries are written as links to Part I material entries, with the per-roll quantity specified. For example, an entry might read: "Mountain Sage — 1d4 bundles", meaning the character rolls 1d4 to determine how many bundles this single resource point produced, and receives that many instances of Mountain Sage with the grade determined by the opportunity roll margin.

Grade at the Point of Harvest

Every material produced by a gathering attempt receives a grade, determined by the margin of the opportunity roll that produced it:

Opportunity Roll Margin Grade
Meet DC to DC + 4 並 Nami — Run-of-the-mill. Standard sample, no bonus, −2 craft modifier.
DC + 5 to DC + 9 上 Jō — Clean and standard. Baseline craft material, +0 modifier.
DC + 10 to DC + 14 特上 Tokujō — High-purity. Notable sample, +2 craft modifier, value ×1.5.
DC + 15 or more 極上 Gokujō — Legendary bloom. The kind of sample master craftsmen remember, +5 or advantage on craft check, value ×2.5.

Natural 20 rule. A natural 20 on the opportunity roll always produces at least one 特上 sample from that attempt, regardless of total margin. The luck goes into finding an exceptional specimen rather than just extra quantity.

Per-Foundry-item implementation. Each grade corresponds to a separate item definition in Foundry (Path D). When a character produces a 特上 Iron Ore on their roll, they receive the "Iron Ore (特上)" item in their inventory — not a generic Iron Ore with a grade tag. Part I entries list all four grade variants in their Grade Variants sub-block with reserved Foundry item IDs.

Legendary and Artifact materials. Most Legendary and Artifact materials do not use the four-grade variant system. They exist as a single canonical grade (usually 極上 or a fixed Legendary designation) because they are tied to specific sources — a Progenitor dragon's scale, the heart of a slain named beast, a sample from a unique location — and rolling quality on them makes no narrative sense. Individual entries specify.

Failure Modes — Gathering

When an opportunity roll fails, the character spent an hour of field time for nothing — and possibly worse. The consequence scales with biome tier.

Biome Tier On Failure On Critical Failure (natural 1)
Accessible 1 hour lost, no yield. 1 hour lost + minor setback — insect bites, torn clothing, a sprained wrist (disadvantage on next physical check).
Wild 1 hour lost + minor complication — bad weather, route unclear, small tool damaged, scavengers in the area. 1 hour lost + tool loss — herbalism kit contaminated, miner's pick snapped, fishing line cut, carpenter's blade chipped.
Hostile 1 hour lost + weather, terrain, or wildlife complication. 1 hour lost + hostile encounter — a CR-appropriate creature drawn by the noise, the smell of blood, or the disturbance to its territory.
Otherworldly 1 hour lost + sei backlash — disadvantage on the next saving throw, eerie attention from unseen watchers, a minor dissociative effect that passes after a short rest. 1 hour lost + major complication — spirit attention from a territorial entity, a cursed or tainted yield that looks valuable but carries a hidden cost, or a CR+2 encounter with something that considers the character's presence an offense.

The DM is encouraged to narrate failures as story beats, not dead ends. The hour is already spent — use it to advance something.

Failure Modes — Crafting

When a craft check fails, the consequence depends on the rarity of the item being made. Lower-tier items are forgiving; higher-tier items are not.

  • Common result — Materials recoverable on failure. The character can try again without cost beyond the time spent.
  • Uncommon result — Half the materials consumed on failure; the other half salvageable for another attempt.
  • Rare result — Most materials consumed on failure. One key component may survive at the DM's discretion, usually tied to a good roleplay moment or a clever use of tools.
  • Very Rare result — Materials fully consumed on failure. The character must re-gather before trying again.
  • Legendary result — Failure destroys all materials and may damage or destroy the tools used. A failed legendary craft is a genuine disaster, narratively and mechanically. The character may suffer reputation or honor consequences.
  • Artifact result — Materials destroyed, tools destroyed or permanently damaged, and the character may suffer a significant narrative consequence: honor loss, spirit backlash, or a lingering curse tied to the wasted material.

Critical failures (natural 1) on craft checks at Rare or above may trigger additional effects at the DM's discretion — a tainted item that looks successful until used, a cursed result, or a partial success with a hidden flaw that only reveals itself in play.

Seasons of Kagekuni

The gathering system uses four seasons plus a set of named seasonal events that transform specific biomes temporarily.

  • Haru 春 — Spring. Budding, young growth, the first fish runs, mountain snowmelt, the opening of foraging season after winter dormancy. Many herbs and wild vegetables are at their most potent in spring. Saishū is productive everywhere; Shuryō is lean until mid-spring when game emerges.
  • Natsu 夏 — Summer. Peak growth, abundance, long days, the heavy rains of tsuyu-no-toki (the rainy window of early summer). Mushroom flushes follow the rains; game is fat and plentiful; the mountain herbs set seed. The best season for most gathering activities in most biomes.
  • Aki 秋 — Autumn. Harvest, rutting season, the falling of bronze and copper leaves in the Seidorin. Kegawa is at its best in autumn when pelts are thick for the coming winter; the final mushroom flushes of the year; the last herbs before dormancy. Hunting is exceptional.
  • Fuyu 冬 — Winter. Dormancy and scarcity. Preserved stores matter most. Saikutsu and Batsuboku are actually easier in winter because vegetation is reduced and access is clearer; Shuryō is harder because animals are wary, hibernating, or gone; Saishū is nearly impossible in most biomes. Some alpine and sei-touched biomes have winter-only yields.

Seasonal Events

Certain biomes transform during named in-world events. These are catalogued here and referenced in the individual biome entries below.

  • Hikarishō 光祥 — The Dragon Aurora. Celestial alignment that produces unique sei conditions across the entire archipelago. During Hikarishō, certain Very Rare materials become temporarily gatherable that are otherwise impossible to find. Hoshimori Kōgen is the most affected biome; secondary effects touch Yōrin and Kazan. Predictable — seimasters at Hoshino Tō can calculate the window.
  • Tatsunami 龍波 — Dragon Wave Season. Nami province phenomenon during which storm swells overwash coastal roads and villages. Standard Kaigan gathering is impossible on Nami's outer coast during this window, but the Stormwatch Cliffs produce unique weather-sei materials for those willing to brave the storms. Dangerous — Hostile biome tier during Tatsunami regardless of the normal rating.
  • Nagaikage 長影 — The Long Shadow. A late-autumn Kusa phenomenon during which the Whispering Flats grow silent in a way locals say allows the dead to speak. Murasaki-hara yields shift — certain grasses and night-blooming plants become gatherable that are otherwise dormant, and some carry spirit-touched properties. Requires local knowledge to exploit; strangers rarely time it right.
  • Compound Low Tide. A recurring coastal event driven by Kagekuni's four-moon tidal system. At compound low tide, the Shirakawa Estuary flats extend for miles, the Tidal Caves of Umigakure become accessible, and the Serenia-kai's shoreline retreats several hundred meters. Kaigan and Uchi-umi yields are exceptional during these windows — materials visible that are normally underwater. The timing is predictable and published in almanacs.

Additional seasonal events will be added to this section as the campaign surfaces them.

The Five Activities — Tool Details

A brief reference on tool proficiencies and what each activity expects.

Saishū 採集 — Herbalism kit grants full opportunity roll with normal advantage rules. Without the kit, a character may still forage but rolls with disadvantage on the opportunity roll. Without any tool, the character can still gather the most obvious surface materials (nuts, berries, obvious mushrooms) at Accessible-tier biomes only, and cannot grade higher than 並 Nami.

Shuryō 狩猟 — Any weapon the character is proficient with. Hunting uses different weapons than fishing — a hunter needs bow or spear; a fisher needs line or net. Specialist equipment (falconry glove, hunting dog, trap kit) may grant advantage at DM discretion when used in the right biome.

Saikutsu 採掘 — Miner's tools (mattock, pick, chisel, wedge) grant full roll. Improvised tools impose disadvantage and cannot produce higher than 上 Jō. Specialist equipment (sei-conductive pick, dwarven stoneworking kit) may grant advantage in specific biomes.

Batsuboku 伐木 — Woodcarver's or carpenter's tools. An axe alone is sufficient for basic timber but cannot produce higher than 上 Jō; full tool kits are required for 特上 and above. A woodcarver's tools are preferred for specialty materials (sei-bark stripping, sap collection); carpenter's tools for structural lumber.

Kaishū 回収 — No tool required, but specialized tools (a torch, a crowbar, a bone saw for scavenging battlefields) may grant advantage in context. The Investigation skill is the core requirement; without proficiency in Investigation, the character may still scavenge but rolls with disadvantage.

Source Types

Beyond the five gathering activities, Part I entries may list a sixth source type: Purchased. This is used for materials that exist in the economy but are not practical to gather in the field — imports from other islands, materials that require industrial-scale processing, or goods controlled by merchant guilds. A Purchased material has no biome or season entries and instead lists the settlements, markets, or trade routes where it is available. Purchased materials never receive grades from gathering rolls; if they are graded at all, the grade is set by the source vendor and reflected in the price.

Biomes of Kagekuni

This section catalogues the gatherable biomes of the Kagekuni archipelago, drawn from the canonical geography. Each entry describes the biome, lists the activities supported, notes which seasons are productive or unproductive, identifies any restrictions or hazards, and houses the yield tables used during play.

Biomes are grouped into three tiers: Core (common biomes every party will hit), Distinctive (unique biomes with specialized yields), and Periphery (stubbed for future build-out).

Phase 3 status. Yield tables have been built for the three priority biomes the current campaign is most likely to hit: Sugi no Mori, Fumoto, and Haikyo (including the Oryuzan Tenku-ji site-specific sub-table). The canonical alias map is preserved in dm/skill-reference.md for any external notes that may still reference the old naming. Any future ingest from external sources should be normalized on import.

Core Biomes

Kaigan 海岸 — Coastal Edge

Headlands, beaches, tidal flats, estuaries, sea caves, and the rugged shorelines of Mizu, Nami, and Hana. The boundary between Kagekuni and the Raijin no Fukai sea. Compound low tides expose materials normally submerged.

Biome Tier: Wild (DC 13) Activities Supported: Saishū, Shuryō, Kaishū Seasonal Notes: All seasons productive; exceptional yields during Compound Low Tide events. Tatsunami makes Nami coast temporarily Hostile. Typical Yields: Shellfish, seaweed, sea salt, driftwood, coastal herbs, shore game, wrecked cargo.

Satoyama 里山 — Village Forest

The managed coppice-edge between settlement and wilderness. The ambient biome around nearly every Kagekuni village. Regular foot traffic keeps the biome thin but accessible; traditional village knowledge keeps productive areas productive.

Biome Tier: Accessible (DC 10) Activities Supported: Saishū, Shuryō (small game only), Batsuboku (coppiced wood) Seasonal Notes: Productive in Haru, Natsu, Aki; poor in Fuyu. Typical Yields: Bamboo, small game (rabbit, fowl), common herbs, mushrooms after rain, firewood.

Sugi no Mori 杉の森 — Deep Cedar Forest

Ancient dense cedar and black pine forest, canopy so thick that sunlight reaches the floor only in scattered shafts. The signature biome of Kaze province, with smaller stretches in Kusa and the Tenchūsan Ren foothills. Mist is constant; navigation relies on landmark and feel more than sight.

Biome Tier: Wild (DC 13) Activities Supported: Saishū, Shuryō, Batsuboku Seasonal Notes: All seasons productive; Kinoko flush best in Natsu after rain (advantage on the yield roll within 24 hours of a rainfall); Kegawa best in Aki (hunters automatically trade up one yield column when the Aki rut is active); Fuyu passable but game scattered. Typical Yields: Large game (deer, boar, occasional bear), rare shade-loving mushrooms, cedar timber, black pine resin, shaded herbs.

Fumoto 麓 — Foothills

The transition zone between lowland and highland, covering the slopes of Sora, the approaches to Tsuchi's mountains, and the edges of the Tenchūsan Ren. The most-traveled biome for parties crossing provinces — every road between coastal lowland and mountain pass runs through Fumoto at some point.

Biome Tier: Wild (DC 13) Activities Supported: Saishū, Shuryō, Saikutsu (surface deposits), Batsuboku Seasonal Notes: All seasons productive except deep Fuyu at higher elevations. Distinctive Biomes

Seidorin 青銅林 — Bronze Wood Forest

The ancient metallic-barked woodland of western Hana. Trees with bark of burnished bronze that chime faintly in the wind and shed their copper leaves in a single night when temperature drops below threshold. Unique endemic flora and fauna. Harvest is regulated by Clan Kaminari under capital-offense penalty.

Biome Tier: Otherworldly (DC 20) Activities Supported: Saishū, Shuryō, Batsuboku (license only) Seasonal Notes: Exceptional Aki yields during the leaf-fall event; otherwise modest but always unique. Restrictions: Unlicensed harvest is a capital offense. Licensed harvest is available only to clan-approved parties under supervision. Penalties apply even for accidental damage. Typical Yields: Bronze-bark timber (licensed only), copper-leaf material, rare endemic herbs and fungi, unique beast products from the silent-canopy fauna.

Yōrin 妖林 — Spirit-Touched Woodland

The sei-active ancient woodland of the Yosei Mori and similar scattered sites. Navigation is unreliable — the forest itself resists mapping. Creatures in deeper reaches show elevated intelligence. The Forest of Spirits faction maintains sanctuaries within.

Biome Tier: Otherworldly (DC 20) Activities Supported: Saishū, Shuryō (with caution — some game here is aware of you), Kaishū (old shrines and forgotten cairns) Seasonal Notes: Sei conditions shift with the seasons unpredictably. Local guides are strongly recommended. Typical Yields: Sei-infused herbs and fungi, spirit-touched water, rare wood from older-than-mapped trees, memory-fragments (Kaishū only, rare).

The tall indigo grasslands of Kusa's interior, including the Whispering Flats. Grass grows chest-high and endemic violet and deep-blue flora gives the landscape its unique character. Exposed and open; navigation easy except in fog.

Tables: TBD

Uchi-umi 内海 — Inland Sea (Serenia-kai)

The vast inland sea of Hana, covering more than a thousand square miles, fed by twenty-five rivers and thirteen waterfalls. Its surface shifts color with the seasons, and compound low tides retreat the shoreline by hundreds of meters, exposing a tidal floor unique in the archipelago.

Biome Tier: Wild (DC 13); Compound Low Tide windows Accessible (DC 10) for easy gathering Activities Supported: Saishū (shoreline and exposed floor), Shuryō (fishing, waterfowl), Kaishū (during compound low tide — exposed wrecks and sealed caves) Seasonal Notes: Color-shift seasons produce unique phenomena; Compound Low Tide events are the gathering prime windows. Typical Yields: Brackish fish, freshwater fish, waterfowl, exposed-floor shellfish, moon-touched water plants, rare finds from compound-tide-exposed shrines.

Tables: TBD

Periphery Biomes

Biomes below are canonized but not yet built out. They will receive full treatment as the campaign approaches them.

Haikyo 廃墟 — Ruins

Promoted to core biome in the Phase 2 materials rework — the party is currently working in the Oryuzan Tenku-ji ruin, and this biome has received its full table build as part of Phase 3.

Haikyo is the scavenging biome — abandoned temples, collapsed observatories, ruined fortresses, pre-imperial sites, burned villages, the Buried Road of Tsuchi, the forgotten outposts of the Dark Ages. Each ruin has its own character, and the Kaishū activity here is far more than picking through rubble — it is historical recovery, sometimes archaeology, sometimes grave-robbing depending on perspective.

Biome Tier: Variable by site — most ruins Wild (DC 13); sei-touched or actively haunted ruins Hostile (DC 16) or Otherworldly (DC 20). Tenku-ji itself is Otherworldly (DC 20) on account of its Golden Dragon Clan preservation magic and sei-active inner chambers. Activities Supported: Kaishū primarily; Saikutsu in worked-stone ruins; occasional Saishū for plants that have overgrown the site. Seasonal Notes: Winter often makes ruins more accessible (vegetation cleared); summer conceals hazards under growth. Restrictions: Varies by site. Temple ruins may be considered sacred by local communities and disturbed at spiritual cost. Clan lands require permission. Imperial-era sites are nominally Kokushi Kyokai jurisdiction. Oryuzan Tenku-ji specifically carries its own set of conditions catalogued in locations/tenkuji-temple/. Typical Yields: Pre-imperial artifacts and tools, forgotten tools and weapons, worked stone, salvaged metal, old documents and scrolls, ceremonial materials, rare finds with attached history. Some ruins yield sei-touched items; some yield cursed ones; a few yield both and the difference is only clear later.

Kaishū — General Haikyo Table

This table applies to any generic Haikyo site — an abandoned watchtower, a burned farmhouse, a pre-imperial cairn, a forgotten way-shrine. The site-specific tables below override individual rows where marked.

Unlike the food-category tables, Haikyo yields are dominated by found objects rather than catalogued materials — scrolls, coins, broken tools, ceremonial fragments — and most entries are narrative placeholders until the matching Part I categories (Kōseki, Sen'i, Mokuzai, Ekitai) are built out. Quantities below are per-resource-point and represent one discrete find per roll.

d20 Result Per-point Yield Column
1 Salvaged iron scrap (pot shards, belt buckles, rusted fittings) 1d4 lb Common
2 Coin cache — mixed mon, a few zeni, occasional ryō fragment 2d6 mon equivalent Common
3 Broken tools — carpenter, farmer, kitchen; some restorable with downtime work 1d3 items Common
4 Worked stone rubble (carved blocks, tile, cut lintel) — value depends on transport 1d4 pieces Common
5 Incidental ceramic — intact pots, plates, a broken inkstone 1d3 items Common
6 Household cloth fragments, moth-eaten bedding, rotted rope 1d4 portions (Sen'i when catalogued) Common
7 Rusted blade or shaft — a broken yari head, a snapped naginata, a bent kodachi; restorable with a smith 1 weapon fragment Common
8 Preserved dried goods — rice bale, miso crock, salted fish — shockingly intact in a sealed cellar. DM decides edibility. 1d3 portions (Shushoku flavor) Common
9 Household shrine remains — a tarnished bell, a broken ofuda, spent incense sticks 1d3 items Common
10 Fungal growth on old timber — Shiitake, Nameko, or Hiratake flush (roll 1d3 to pick) 1d3 caps Common
11 Intact tool or implement — a planemaker's kanna, a bronze tea whisk, a brass lantern hook — salvage quality is jō (上) at minimum 1 item Uncommon
12 Old documents — fragmentary scrolls, ledger pages, a burned letter; may carry campaign-relevant information at DM discretion 1d3 fragments Uncommon
13 Kageboushi (影帽子) — growing in lightless galleries, cellars, collapsed voids 1d2 caps Uncommon
14 Sealed container — a lacquer box, a sealed ceramic jar, a locked chest with contents intact; DM rolls 1d6 on sub-table or improvises 1 container Uncommon
15 Worked bronze fittings — door pulls, temple hinges, decorative inlay — prized by smiths as reclamation stock 1d4 lb Uncommon
16 Preserved silk — a folded kosode, a banner, a ceremonial wrap — colours still holding 1 garment / banner Uncommon
17 Intact weapon — an unbroken wakizashi, a strung yumi with sinew still taut, a quiver of arrows; condition varies but the object is usable 1 weapon Uncommon
18 Yūrei-kusa (幽霊草) — ghost grass growing on truly abandoned ground, on spots where something terrible happened 1d2 bundles Rare
19 Sealed-chamber preservation — a chamber the rain never reached. Contents untouched for years. DM discretion on contents — a single focused find that advances the campaign is better than generic treasure. 1 discrete find Rare
20 Site-specific anomaly — roll on the site-specific sub-table below if applicable; otherwise DM introduces a discovery that drives a new plot thread, lore reveal, or character moment. Haikyo Very Rare yields are almost always story-first. varies Very Rare (requires unlock)
Kaishū — Oryuzan Tenku-ji (Site-Specific)

The party is currently working this site. Tenku-ji's yield table overrides the generic Haikyo table in specific ways — the temple's preservation magic kept certain chambers intact across millennia, and its Golden Dragon Clan heritage means that genuine relics of the First Golden Age still surface in protected zones. Conversely, the Nagaji occupation has stripped most exposed chambers of anything portable. Loot density is bimodal: common/open areas yield almost nothing (don't reward casual searching), but sealed, collapsed, or preserved chambers yield exceptional finds.

Tier modifier: Tenku-ji is Otherworldly (DC 20). A character succeeding on the opportunity roll with margin 15+ unlocks the Very Rare column automatically.

Table substitutions for Tenku-ji (replaces the equivalent rows of the General Haikyo table above):

d20 Result Per-point Yield Column
1–3 No find. The Nagaji have already picked this area over, or the chamber has decayed to nothing usable. Mark the hour spent. (The Tenku-ji Loot Framework canonically suppresses common-area yields.) 0 Common
4 Kinryū tile fragment — a palm-sized shard of the gold-leaf mosaic that once covered the Grand Hall's upper walls. Collectible, sacred, and tracked. 1 fragment Common
5 Fungal growth on ancient timber — Shiitake, Nameko, or Hiratake (roll 1d3) in moisture-sealed corners 1d3 caps Common
6 Dragon-priest brush-fragment — a snapped calligraphy brush with hair still intact and a scraped ink stone; working order with restoration 1 item Common
7 Preserved ritual cord — fragments of shimenawa, rope of unusual fibre weave, woven silver thread in small amounts 1d3 fragments (Sen'i-adjacent) Common
8 Broken temple bronze — worn lantern hooks, hinges, decorative fittings with Kinryū iconography 1d4 lb Common
9 Coin cache — Golden Age denominations, mixed with later pieces, occasionally a ryū-mon unique to the Golden Dragon Clan 2d6 mon equivalent + 1d4 ryū-mon (collector value) Common
10 Kageboushi (影帽子) — growing in lightless galleries behind collapsed masonry 1d2 caps Common
11 Preserved scroll fragment — a single page of temple record, ritual instruction, or astronomical calculation; may carry [DISCOVERABLE] lore at DM discretion 1 fragment Uncommon
12 Intact ceremonial implement — a bronze offering bowl, a jade incense stick rest, a carved haishaku (ritual dipper) — Golden Clan provenance 1 item Uncommon
13 Preservation-magic-touched object — an item that has simply not aged: a folded robe in perfect condition, a sealed bottle of water with impossible clarity, a lamp still holding oil. Handle with care and archive appropriately. 1 item Uncommon
14 Ryūsō (竜草) — Dragon Herb, growing only at Progenitor shrine sites. Tenku-ji's foundation retained enough of Kinryū's touch to support it. 1d2 bundles Uncommon
15 Intact Dragon Clan weapon — an heirloom-quality katana, yari, or naginata with Kinryū motif, condition preserved 1 weapon Uncommon
16 Sealed record — a lacquered scroll tube, a carved wooden box, a banded chest containing preserved documents. A genuine find of archival significance. DM discretion on contents. 1 container Uncommon
17 Star-shrine fragment — a shard of the constellation-casting array, a worn astronomical instrument, a calibration plate from the upper observatory. Very useful to a seimaster. 1 item Uncommon
18 Ryūketsu-bana (竜血花) — Dragon's Blood Flower. The only place in Hokori where it grows in living condition rather than dried. 1d2 flowers Rare
19 Preserved relic chamber — a chamber sealed by preservation magic still holds its original contents. DM places a single meaningful object: a reliquary, a ritual weapon, a record, a crystal focus. This is a campaign find, not a yield. 1 discrete campaign find Rare
20 Kinryū-touched find — DM discretion. The search has found something directly connected to the Golden Dragon himself: a scale fragment, a Progenitor-era prayer inscription, a sei-resonant artifact that hums when held. Resolves as a story beat with long-term mechanical significance. 1 discrete campaign find Very Rare (requires unlock)

DM guidance — Tenku-ji yield philosophy. Do not roll this table casually. The room files in locations/tenkuji-temple/floor-1/ define where specific finds exist canonically — those placements take precedence over yield rolls. This table is for the spaces between the canonized rooms: the pillars the party chose to chip at, the rubble they decided to clear, the ducts they squeezed through without narrative intent. A rolled find should reinforce the preservation-vs-decay duality of the temple, not dilute it.

Saikutsu — Tenku-ji Worked-Stone Recovery

Tenku-ji's worked stone is unusually dense — the Golden Dragon Clan used a basalt-granite composite still unknown to modern stonemasons. Saikutsu attempts within the temple grounds yield:

  • 1 resource point = 1d4 lb of reclamation stone (ordinary reuse value)
  • On a nat-20 opportunity roll: one worked Kinryū-iconography block suitable for direct reuse in an active shrine (rare, high collector value — see DM notes)

Full table stubbed pending Kōseki build-out.

Saishū — Overgrown Tenku-ji

The outer courtyards and lower terraces have been reclaimed by the Tenchūsan Ren forest over millennia. A brief Saishū pass catches the overlap zone where Haikyo meets Sugi no Mori / Takane:

  • Roll on the Sugi no Mori Saishū table with the following modifiers:
    • Row 20 (Very Rare) — if unlocked, automatically yields Ryūsō (竜草) instead of the generic spirit-touched substitute, reflecting the temple's Progenitor resonance.
    • Rows 18–19 gain a 1-in-3 chance to substitute Ryūketsu-bana (竜血花) — a find of genuine campaign significance.
  • Alpine strays from Takane (Ginrei-sō, Iwa-ninniku) may appear in the upper-terrace slot on DM discretion.

Kōri-no-Mori 氷の森 — Frozen Forest

Mizu's northern frost-touched woodland. Stubbed until the party reaches it.

Biome Tier: Hostile (DC 16) Tables: TBD

Ōumi 大海 — Open Sea

Deep-water fishing and leviathan territory. Relevant when the party takes to ships.

Biome Tier: Hostile (DC 16); storm conditions Otherworldly (DC 20) Tables: TBD

Kuroso Kōya 黒瀬荒野 — Obsidian Wasteland

The specific Hi sub-biome of the vast obsidian plains. May be treated as a sub-area of Kazan or given its own table at a later phase depending on how often it surfaces in play.

Biome Tier: Otherworldly (DC 20) Tables: TBD

Cross-Biome Tags

A cross-biome tag is not a physical biome — it cannot be pointed to on a map and does not replace a biome entry on a material. It is a descriptor that modifies an existing biome to mark a distinct mode of presence. A material tagged with a cross-biome tag must also carry a physical biome (Sugi no Mori, Kaigan, Haikyo, etc.); the tag identifies which subset of that biome's sites produce the yield.

The gathering mechanic treats a tag as a tier escalator and a frequency gate: a cross-biome-tagged site is typically at least Hostile (DC 16) and often Otherworldly (DC 20), and such sites are rare enough that a party should feel finding one is an event, not a routine travel stop.

Spirit-Touched (精霊触れ)

Sei flows visibly through a Spirit-Touched site. The tag covers any location where raw sei has pooled, lingered, or bled into the material world strongly enough to alter what grows, lives, and settles there. Examples of qualifying sites include: Progenitor caverns, active shrine pools, the Yōsei Mori's oldest hardwoods, the Seidōrin Mori interior, the Hoshimori Plateau during Hikarishō, and Ginryū-associated mineral sites. The tag does not apply to routine shrine grounds — sei must be actively perceptible, not merely venerated.

Tier default: Otherworldly (DC 20) at the tagged site, regardless of the underlying biome's base tier. A Spirit-Touched Kaigan grotto is treated at DC 20 even though generic Kaigan is Wild. Activity effects: Yield tables for the underlying biome apply normally, but the Very Rare column (row 20) is considered thematically unlocked at Spirit-Touched sites — a margin-15 opportunity roll at such a site is almost certain to produce a sei-resonant result. Restrictions: Most Spirit-Touched sites sit within another faction's claim (Forest of Spirits, Hoshimori seimasters, Dragon Clan shrine remnants) or under spirit-world attention. Unauthorized harvest frequently triggers consequences that land outside the gathering system — quests, curses, or direct response. DM guidance: Spirit-Touched is the mechanism by which a handful of materials (Ryūsō, Yūrei-kusa variants, Hoshimori silver-grass, Progenitor-cavern crystals) can appear across otherwise unrelated physical biomes without breaking the biome taxonomy. Use it sparingly — the tag loses meaning if every sei-active rock qualifies.

Named Beast Harvests

One-time legendary yields from slain named creatures. Components are catalogued in their respective Part I categories in the standard schema; this section cross-references them by source beast so a DM can answer "what did the party get from killing X" in a single lookup.

Yama-no-Ōkami (Slain)

Event. The Yama-no-Ōkami — Mountain God of the Tenchūsan Ren — was slain during the Fushichō ashfall in the mountain pass. A Huge-category beast, roughly 12–15 feet from nose to haunch, 8 feet at the shoulder, between 6,000 and 8,000 pounds. Butchered with exceptional skill: the natural 20 on the harvest check triggered the bonus d10 and cleared the Legendary threshold, securing every cut the beast had to offer, including the Reikokoro.

Grade lock. All Yama-no-Ōkami components are single-grade-locked at 極上 Gokujō. The nat-20 harvest check locked every component at top grade at the moment of butchering; no lesser grade exists for any of this beast's material. Entries for these components do not carry the standard Nami/Jō/Tokujō/Gokujō Grade Variants table — the 極上 row stands alone.

Components by category. The full harvest is catalogued across five Part I categories. Cross-references:

Category Component Yield Tracked
Niku Ōkami-niku (Mountain God's Flesh) 8 portions ✓
Niku Shirokiba no Zui (White-Fang Marrow) 3 portions ✓
Niku Yama no Kimo (Mountain Liver) 2 portions ✓
Niku Arashi-suji (Storm-Sinew) 3 portions ✓
Niku Reikokoro (Spirit Heart) — Legendary 1 portion (feeds six) ✓
Shushoku Ōkami no Abura (Rendered Fat) 6 portions ✓
Kegawa Ōkami no Kegawa (Pelt) 1 primary + 2 secondary sections ✓
Hone Ōkami no Hone (Bones) ~350 lb carving stock ✓
Hone Ōkami no Zugai (Skull) 1 intact skull ✓
Hone Ōkami no Kiba (Fangs) 4 fangs ✓
Hone Ōkami no Tenohira (Paws) 4 paws (20 claws total) ✓

Tracking. The party currently holds all of the above. Consumption, sale, gift, and enshrinement should be recorded against dm/campaign-state.md, not against this file. When a component is exhausted, strike it through here but leave the Part I entry intact for historical reference.

Skill-check knowledge. The non-food components (Kegawa and Hone categories) each carry DM-only Religion / Nature / Arcana reveal thresholds. See the DM Notes block of each individual component entry for the specific DCs and what each check reveals. A natural 20 on any one check reveals the information across all three skills for that component.

The Reikokoro. The Spirit Heart is unique even among the Yama-no-Ōkami components — it is the only entry in the entire harvest catalogued at the Legendary tier rather than 極上 Gokujō. It feeds up to six generously from a single preparation and is suitable for a Masterwork dish. Religion, Nature, and Arcana reveals on the Reikokoro are documented with the Niku entry and should be read before the party considers consuming it.

Appendix — Document Maintenance

Source of truth. This file is canonical. When conflicts arise between materials.md and other files (recipes.md, lore-index.md, campaign-state.md, the Sanzai Campaign Guide), this file wins for material definitions and gathering mechanics.

Reindex integration. The reindex skill is responsible for rebuilding the "Used In" section of each Part I entry by crawling core/recipes.md and any future split recipe files. This section is regenerated on every reindex pass. Do not edit Used In manually.

Foundry export. When a Foundry export pipeline is built, it will read Part I entries and generate four item definitions per graded material (Path D). The Grade Variants sub-block reserves the Foundry item ID slots. Player-facing fields (Description, Unidentified Description, Image Prompt) become the item's visible properties. DM Notes are excluded from export.

Schema evolution. If the Part I entry schema changes, all existing entries must be updated in the same pass to maintain consistency. A schema change without a full sweep is a source-of-truth corruption.

Knowledge tier enforcement. Never surface [DISCOVERABLE] or [SEALED] content in player-facing fields. The description and unidentified description fields are exports; DM Notes is the only safe home for tiered content.

text.content:
Government & Political Structure

Hierarchy

Emperor → Shogun (war appointment only) → Kokushi Kyōkai → Daimyo → Rōjū

Current Status

  • Emperor: Dead since 16739; no confirmed successor; multiple claimants with sketchy genealogical proof
  • Shogun: Position legally frozen — Ryūjin's 16732 reform requires imperial approval; no emperor to grant it
  • Kokushi Kyōkai: Functioning but rudderless; Daijin are holdovers in constitutional limbo
  • Active War: Genso Alliance vs Arashi Alliance since 16742

The Five Daijin (Currently Holdovers)

Title Role
Anzen Hoshō Daijin Minister of Security — intelligence network, imperial protectorate
Fukushi Daijin Minister of Welfare — healthcare, education, public assistance
Gaikō Daijin Minister of Foreign Affairs — diplomacy, trade, foreign nationals
Seimu Daijin Minister of Administration — provincial governance, infrastructure
Zaiumu Daijin Minister of Finance — treasury, taxation, revenue

Local Administration Chain

Chiji (Governor) → Gunji (County Magistrate) → Shi (Municipal Assembly) → Shicho (Mayor) → Sonchō (Village Leader)

Teikoku Keisatsu (Imperial Police)

  • Functioning law enforcement bureaucracy
  • With no emperor, has retreated to regional/local footprint
  • Operates with some cooperation with local forces
  • Chief Inspector Oshiro Masahiro stationed in Ayame — confirmed party ally

Military Structure

Command Hierarchy

Shogun → Daimyo → Sotaisho → Karo → Taisho → Kumigashira → Kogashira

Enlisted (Ashigaru) — Peasant Infantry

  • Katana Ashigaru (sword)
  • Yari Ashigaru (spear)
  • Yumi Ashigaru (bow)

Samurai Ranks (Low to High)

  • Gokenin — housemen
  • Goshi — rustic warrior
  • Hatamoto — bannerman

Bugyo — Logistics Officers

Sobugyo (field marshal), Maku bugyō, Yari/Yumi/Teppō/Kakomi bugyō (weapons commissioners), Yoroi bugyō (armor), Shodōgu bugyō (equipment), Hata bugyō (flags), Hyōrō bugyō (provisions), Gozen bugyō (kitchen), Fune bugyō (boats)

Ronin Surge

With political vacuum and clan warfare, ronin numbers are at an all-time high — masterless samurai available for recruitment by any faction.

Caste & Social System

Three Castes

Kugai — Elite class

  • Primarily humans and dragonborn claiming descent from imperial founders
  • Daimyo, Courtiers, Scholars, Hatamoto

Zokumin — Commonfolk

  • Mixed races and ethnicities; varying regional acceptance
  • Samurai, Ronin, Peasants, Artisans, Merchants (descending order)
  • Merchants lowest despite often considerable wealth — source of social tension

Burakumin — Outcasts

  • Occupations involving death (leather workers, butchers, executioners, undertakers)
  • Segregated buraku communities; limited civil rights
  • Subject to systemic harassment

Racial Social Mechanics

Characters who are not Dragonborn, Human, or the clan's dominant non-human race suffer -2 on Honor ability checks due to systemic racism. Conversely, marginalized characters may be underestimated — opportunities to gather secrets others would guard more carefully.

The Clans

Alliance Structure

Alliance Clans
Arashi Arashiyama, Hoshizora, Shirotsuru, Yūgure
Genso Fuyugiri, Homoruyama, Ryūkaze, Tsuchiura
Independent Gekkō, Kaminari, Kurohana

The three independents are the political wildcard — their allegiance could tip the conflict decisively.

Clan Kaminari

  • Daimyo: Raijin no Kazuhiko (The Storm-lord; human; 47; black hair with silver streaks)
  • Known for mastery of storm magic and fierce warriors
  • Born outside the clan; rose through martial prowess
  • Governs Province of Hana; capital Heian

Clan Kurohana (Independent)

  • Daimyo: Akihiko Kurohana (Black Dragonborn; 54; black scales; glowing red eyes; 6'6")

Other Notable Clans

  • Clan Tsuchiura: Governs Mizuho region, Tatara
  • Clan Shirotsuru: Governs Shugyoku region, Tatara (Arashi Alliance)
  • Eikyū Yami Clan: Kuroyami's dark cult; status unclear but persists

Clan Seishin (Minor — Subject of Kaminari)

  • Daimyo: Ren Nakamura (Shicho of Kikyo; human; 52)
  • Also known as Clan Minato for his lesser clan title
  • Secret: Working to elevate Clan Seishin/Minato; secret alliance with merchant guild
  • Possesses ancient knowledge about Seidōrin Mori and Bronze Wood

• Secret: Kazuhiko doubts accusations against Dian's father; investigating emperor's assassination

  • Key personnel: Hideo Nakamura (Taisho/Special Ops), Hiroshi Nakamura (Taisho/Shugo of Heian — TRAITOR), Arinori Senzai (Hyōrō Bugyō), Haruto Masashige (Captain of Guard, Kikyo)

  • Secret: Doubts accusations against Dian's father; investigating emperor's assassination

  • Issued Imperial Seal calling for Gekkō investigation

  • Key personnel: Noboru Takeda (incompetent mid-level commander), Tatsuya Hoshino (loyal samurai)

Clan Gekkō (Independent — COMPROMISED)

  • Daimyo: Masota no Gekkō — missing; transformed by dark ritual
  • CRITICAL SECRET: Clan Gekkō attempted a dark ritual with catastrophic consequences — clan members transformed into Nagaji (serpent folk)
  • Masota no Gekkō was also transformed
  • Full truth to be revealed at Monastery of the Black Lily in Akatsuki, Kaze province
  • The Nagaji the party has been encountering ARE Clan Gekkō members
  • Party has killed several without knowing they were people — moral weight pending
